findings.title: Unpinned remote script piped to sh in Docker build
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 3 executes `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` during `docker build`. The downloaded script is neither version-pinned nor integrity-checked (no checksum/signature), and `curl` runs without `--fail`, so any HTTP error body or a compromised/DNS-hijacked endpoint is fed straight into `sh`. Whatever the URL's operator (or anyone able to tamper with that response) returns runs with the build user's privileges and any build-time secrets, and the resulting image silently bakes in that arbitrary code. Because the content is mutable at a URL with no digest, the same Dockerfile can produce different, untrustworthy images over time (non-reproducible, unreviewable supply chain).

findings.title: Do not pipe unpinned remote script into root shell at build time
findings.whyItBreaks: `RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` executes whatever the remote server returns as root inside the image build. There is no version pin, no checksum/signature verification, and no pinned commit/tag, so the build is non-reproducible and any compromise or content change at that URL (or an upstream redirect) silently becomes arbitrary code execution in the produced image. It also fetches from example.com, a reserved documentation domain (RFC 2606) that does not host install.sh: the URL returns HTML/404, which is then fed to `sh`, so the step either fails the build or executes garbage. This is unreviewable remote code with full build-time privileges.

findings.title: curl failure is masked by pipe, silently producing broken image
findings.whyItBreaks: In `RUN curl -sL ... | sh` the pipeline exit status is `sh`'s status, and `curl` is invoked without `-f`/`--fail` and the shell without `set -o pipefail`. If the download fails (network error, DNS failure, or an HTTP 4xx/5xx error page), curl exits non-zero but is ignored; `sh` receives empty or error-HTML input and typically exits 0, so the Docker build succeeds and ships an image where the intended install silently never happened. The failure is indistinguishable from success in the final layer.

findings.title: Do not pipe unpinned remote install.sh into root shell at build
findings.whyItBreaks: `RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` executes whatever the server returns as root inside the image build, with no integrity verification: no pinned version, no SHA-256 checksum, no TLS pinning, and `-s` suppresses transfer errors while the absence of `-f` means an HTTP 404/redirect body is still piped to `sh`. A compromised DNS/CDN/host or a mutable `install.sh` turns every build into arbitrary code execution in the image that ships to production. It is also unreviewable and non-reproducible: the artifact is fetched fresh each build, so the image contents cannot be audited from the repo and can change silently.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing and makes failure indistinguishable
findings.whyItBreaks: The added exported function discards the error from Load (`v, _ := Load(key, m)`) and returns the zero value "". A missing key (Load returns "", ErrMissing at src/store.go:9-11) and a key that is genuinely present with value "" (Load returns "", nil at src/store.go:12) both produce "". Because the public signature returns only string, no caller can detect, log, or branch on the lookup failure. Any future caller that uses this result to gate persistence, routing, validation, or an approval decision is forced to act on an empty string as though it were real data. This is an added public path that discards an error signal, so it is a defect in the exported contract itself even though there are no in-repo callers yet.

findings.title: Don't swallow ErrMissing in exported LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: LoadOrDefault ignores the error returned by Load at line 16 (`v, _ := Load(key, m)`) and returns the zero value "". Load signals a missing key via ErrMissing (returned at line 10), which is now indistinguishable from a key that is present with an intentionally empty value. The helper is exported and has no doc/type contract declaring that missing==empty, so every eventual caller is forced to treat a failed lookup as real data (e.g. a missing required config entry silently resolves to ""). The name also promises an "OrDefault" behavior, but the signature exposes no default parameter, so callers cannot supply one.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing, conflating missing key with empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: Load (src/store.go:7-13) returns ("", ErrMissing) when the key is absent and (v, nil) only when the key is present. LoadOrDefault at line 16 does `v, _ := Load(key, m)`, discarding the error, and returns only the string. Because a present key may legitimately map to "", the returned value "" is indistinguishable between 'key absent' and 'key present with empty value'. Since LoadOrDefault is exported, there is no error channel at all: any future caller that needs to tell absence from an empty value (e.g. to apply a real default, reject a missing config, or skip a write) cannot, and will silently act on the fallback as if it were the stored value. Per the swallowed-failure rule an exported swallow site is a defect even with no in-repo callers; the repository currently has none (rg confirms), so the API contract itself is the defect.

findings.title: Add WaitGroup: Run now returns before goroutines send results
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, Run blocked until every job had been sent to `results`, so on return all sends were complete and were enqueued in job order. Now each iteration spawns a detached goroutine and the loop finishes immediately, so Run can return having delivered zero results. Because `results` is send-only and there is no WaitGroup (and `ctx` is never selected on), the caller has no way to learn when the goroutines finish. A caller that follows the natural pattern of closing `results` after Run returns will race the goroutines and panic with `send on closed channel`; a caller ranging over `results` can also observe a randomized order instead of jobs order. There is no error signal to propagate here, but the public function's implicit completion contract is now unfulfillable.

findings.title: Run returns before goroutines send; close(results) now panics
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, every `results <- j*2` completed before Run returned, so `worker.Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)` (or any caller that assumes Run means 'all jobs done') was safe. Now the sends happen in detached goroutines and Run returns immediately with no WaitGroup or done signal. A caller using the previously-safe pattern closes results while goroutines are still blocked in `results <- j * 2`, producing `panic: send on closed channel` (a nondeterministic data race on the close/send ordering). Callers also have no way to know when all results have been delivered.

findings.title: Concurrent sends drop deterministic result ordering
findings.whyItBreaks: The base loop emitted results in the same order as `jobs`; because results carry only the doubled value (no job index), ordering was the only way for a consumer to correlate a result with its input job. Goroutine scheduling makes the send order nondeterministic, so any consumer that zips results back against jobs gets mismatched values. This is an unannounced behavioral change to an exported API.

findings.title: Run returns before goroutines send; callers can panic or lose results
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change Run sent every j*2 synchronously, so its postcondition was 'all len(jobs) results have been handed to results' by the time it returned. Now it only launches one goroutine per job and returns immediately, so that postcondition no longer holds. Any caller using the idiomatic pattern `ch := make(chan int, len(jobs)); Run(ctx, jobs, ch); close(ch); for r := range ch {}` (or a `defer close(ch)`) will close results while goroutines are still executing line 8, producing a 'send on closed channel' panic; a caller that starts a reader after Run returns may simply observe fewer than len(jobs) values or zero if main exits before the goroutines run. Result ordering (previously job order) is also no longer guaranteed. Run is an exported function, so this altered completion contract affects every caller even though none exist in this repo.

findings.title: Unbounded goroutine fan-out replaces channel backpressure
findings.whyItBreaks: One goroutine is spawned per element of jobs with no bound and no coordination. Previously a slow or stalled consumer applied backpressure because Run blocked on the synchronous send at line 8; now Run returns instantly and every pending job has a live goroutine blocked on `results <-`, so a large jobs slice causes unbounded concurrency and, if the receiver stops draining, a permanent goroutine leak. The passed ctx is never consulted, so a cancelled/deadline-bearing caller cannot stop the fan-out or the blocked sends.

findings.title: Fix authorization bypass: OR grants delete to non-admins and cross-tenant admins
findings.whyItBreaks: Replacing `&&` with `||` inverts the two independent requirements into alternatives. Before this PR only an admin in the record's own tenant could delete (`session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId`). Now `session.isAdmin || session.tenantId === record.tenantId` returns true in two illegitimate cases: (1) a non-admin user whose tenantId matches any record in the tenant can delete records they do not own (horizontal privilege escalation), and (2) an admin from any tenant can delete another tenant's records (tenant-isolation bypass). Any delete endpoint that gates on this exported predicate will now perform unauthorized deletions, i.e. a data-loss/security bypass.

findings.title: Revert OR to AND in canDeleteRecord — auth bypass
findings.whyItBreaks: The delete-authorization predicate was weakened from conjunction to disjunction. Previously a delete was allowed only for an admin whose tenant matched the record tenant (session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId). Now `session.isAdmin || session.tenantId === record.tenantId` allows (a) any non-admin user to delete records in their own tenant (privilege escalation) and (b) any admin to delete records belonging to other tenants (cross-tenant data destruction). Both are authorization bypasses on a destructive operation on an exported public function.

findings.title: AND→OR in canDeleteRecord grants cross-tenant and non-admin deletes
findings.whyItBreaks: The original `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId` required BOTH admin status AND tenant match. With `||` the condition short-circuits: (1) `session.isAdmin === true` alone returns true, so an admin may delete records belonging to ANY other tenant — a tenant-isolation/authorization bypass enabling cross-tenant data destruction; (2) a non-admin whose `session.tenantId === record.tenantId` now passes, so any ordinary user in the tenant may delete any record in it — the `ownerId` field is never consulted, so even records they do not own are deletable. This is a strict broadening of an exported authorization predicate; every consumer that trusts canDeleteRecord to gate a destructive delete will now permit actions it previously denied.

findings.title: parseSettings swallow makes updateFontSize clobber corrupt settings with defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, a JSON.parse failure or a bad theme/fontSize threw out of parseSettings and propagated through updateFontSize, so save() was never called and the caller could surface the error. Now every failure is mapped to a legitimate value ({theme:"light",fontSize:14}). updateFontSize (line 20) cannot distinguish 'invalid raw' from 'valid settings', so it mutates fontSize on the fallback and calls save() at line 22, overwriting the stored settings and resetting a valid theme (e.g. "dark") to "light". That is silent user-data loss on a real persisted file, and the error signal is gone at every decision point.

findings.title: Don't swallow parse errors and overwrite stored settings with defaults

The only in-repo caller, updateFontSize (line 20), reads that fallback, sets fontSize, and calls save (line 22). Before this change parseSettings threw on invalid JSON or wrong field types, so updateFontSize propagated the error and never reached save. Now, for a stored value such as raw='{"theme":"dark","fontSize":"14"}', parseSettings returns {...DEFAULTS} and the next font-size update persists {theme:'light',fontSize:<size>}, silently discarding the user's theme. Failure and the fallback are not distinguishable to the caller, so the fallback is written as if it were the user's real settings.

findings.title: Empty catch in parseSettings hides errors and persists defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change parseSettings threw on malformed JSON or an invalid theme/fontSize, so callers could detect corruption and avoid overwriting stored settings. The only in-repo caller, updateFontSize (line 20), then does `save(JSON.stringify(settings))` (line 22), so a partially-valid/legacy config such as `{"theme":"dark"}` (missing fontSize) or truncated/corrupt JSON is silently rewritten as `{"theme":"light","fontSize":N}` — the user's theme preference is lost and the corruption is undetectable. Because parseSettings is exported, any external caller is likewise forced to conflate 'parse failed' with 'a legitimately default-valued config'.

findings.title: Revert pageCount to Math.ceil — floor drops the last partial page
findings.whyItBreaks: pageCount must report the number of pages needed to cover all items, so a partial final page must round up. With Math.floor, pageCount(10, 3) returns 3 while 4 pages are required to hold all 10 items; the 10th item falls outside every computed page. This is a public exported function whose name and prior behavior promise a complete page count, so any caller sizing a page loop or pagination control will silently truncate results.

findings.title: buildReport returns artifacts from a different commit than builtFrom
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport(build, branch) resolves commit = build.ref(branch) and reports it as builtFrom, but the added line resolves verified = build.ref("verified") and passes that to build.artifactsAt. The returned BuildReport therefore lists the artifacts of the "verified" ref next to the branch's commit. Whenever the branch tip and the "verified" ref do not point at the same commit, the artifact list does not describe the commit the report claims to be built from; a caller that displays or acts on builtFrom + artifacts gets a mismatched/wrong artifact set. Before this change the artifacts were correctly taken at commit (build.artifactsAt(commit)), so this is a behavioral regression.

findings.title: Report artifacts no longer match the reported builtFrom commit
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR the same value (commit = build.ref(branch)) fed both the `builtFrom` field and `build.artifactsAt(...)`, so the artifact list always corresponded to the commit the report claimed to be built from. The change introduces `const verified = build.ref("verified")` and passes it to `artifactsAt`, but `builtFrom` still carries `commit`. On any build where the branch ref and the `verified` ref differ, buildReport now returns an artifact list resolved from a different revision than `builtFrom` advertises -- the report silently misattributes artifacts (e.g. reporting artifacts of the verified/promoted revision as if they belonged to the branch build). This is a user-facing output regression for every consumer of BuildReport.

findings.title: buildReport pairs builtFrom branch commit with artifacts from other ref
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR the same commit drove both fields: `const commit = build.ref(branch); return { builtFrom: commit, artifacts: build.artifactsAt(commit) }`. The PR keeps `builtFrom: commit` but reads a second, hardcoded ref `verified = build.ref("verified")` and returns `artifacts: build.artifactsAt(verified)`. The branch argument is now honored only for the label; the artifact list comes from whatever `ref("verified")` points at. Whenever the 'verified' ref differs from the branch tip (the normal reason to resolve a separate ref), the report advertises artifacts as belonging to `builtFrom`/branch while listing artifacts from a different commit, so any consumer that trusts the report to locate/verify artifacts for the reported commit acts on the wrong revision. The previous behavior was consistent; this is a regression introduced by the change.

findings.title: recentEntries ignores limit and returns all entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The doc comment at src/feed.ts:1 promises "at most `limit` entries", but the new body computes `sorted = [...all].reverse()` and then `return sorted` for every `limit > 0`, never applying `.slice(0, limit)`. Only `limit <= 0` is handled (returns []). The sole caller, renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9), passes limit=20 and relies on the bound: it allocates `new Array<string>(20)` (line 10) and loops `for (let i = 0; i < page.length; i++) out[i] = page[i]` (line 11). With the bug, if `all` has N>20 entries, page.length=N, so the loop keeps assigning past index 19 and JS grows `out` to N — renderFeed returns N entries instead of 20, an unbounded/user-visible feed. The old `.slice(0, limit)` returned exactly the newest `limit`; this is a regression introduced by this diff. (For `limit < 0` behavior also changed from "all but last |limit|" to [], but the positive-limit contract violation is the substantive defect.)

findings.title: recentEntries ignores limit and returns all entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The doc contract at src/feed.ts:1 promises "at most `limit` entries, newest first", and the previous body did `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)`. The new body builds `sorted` then `return sorted;` for every `limit > 0`, so the slice is gone: recentEntries(all, 20) now returns the entire (reversed) array. The only in-repo caller renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9) passes 20 and then does `const out = new Array<string>(20); for (let i = 0; i < page.length; i++) out[i] = page[i];` (lines 10-11). Because assigning out[i] for i >= 20 grows a JS array, renderFeed now returns all entries instead of at most 20, violating the documented feed size and removing the cap.

findings.title: recentEntries no longer enforces limit; returns all entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The old body was `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)`. The new body reverses into `sorted`, adds a `limit <= 0` early-out, but returns `sorted` unchanged. For any limit > 0 the `limit` cap is never applied, so `recentEntries(all, limit)` returns `all.length` entries (reversed) instead of at most `limit`. This contradicts the unchanged doc contract on line 1 ("Returns at most `limit` entries, newest first"). The in-repo consumer `renderFeed` (line 9) calls `recentEntries(all, 20)` and then sizes/loops on `page.length` (lines 10-11); with more than 20 inputs `page.length` exceeds 20, the loop writes past the intended 20 slots, and `out` grows to `all.length`, so the feed silently returns an unbounded list instead of a 20-entry page.

findings.title: Manifest entry-count no longer matches emitted rows
findings.whyItBreaks: This PR filters out stale entries into `live` (line 20) and builds rows from `live` (line 21), but line 22 still passes `entries.length` to headerLines. The emitted `# entry-count: N` therefore counts all input entries, including stale ones, while the body contains only non-stale rows. Before this change rows and count always agreed (both used `entries`), so this is a regression introduced here. Any consumer that trusts `# entry-count` (to size/validate the row set or to detect truncation) now sees a count larger than the actual number of data lines. For an exported output contract, the header promise itself is the defect.

findings.title: entry-count header includes stale entries no longer rendered

With any stale entry present the emitted manifest header claims more entries than it lists. Example: entries=[{path:'a',size:1,stale:false},{path:'b',size:2,stale:true}] yields `# entry-count: 2` followed by a single tab-separated row, so a consumer that trusts entry-count to size/verify the row set sees a mismatch (or an out-of-range read). The header is an unchanged promise whose body no longer honors it — Trigger C contract drift.

findings.title: entry-count header counts stale entries excluded from rows

For any input containing a stale entry, `# entry-count: N` reports a larger number than the number of entry rows actually emitted. Before this change both used the full list and stayed consistent; the change introduces a self-contradictory manifest. Any consumer that trusts the count (row expected, batch sizing, diff/validator) sees an off-by-stale mismatch.

The change replaces a working pure transformation with a guaranteed runtime failure, i.e. an unusable core path with no fallback or feature flag.

findings.title: Payment check in canProceed blocks saving unpaid drafts
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is a shared predicate read by two distinct actions: submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) and saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9). Saving a draft is a legitimate action independent of payment, so requiring payment to save it is an over-block and a user-facing regression. submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) is legitimately governed by the payment state, but saveDraft is not.

findings.title: Read snapshot files from requested channel, not hardcoded stable
findings.whyItBreaks: The function still reports `commit: head` (the requested channel's head from `repo.headCommit(channel)`) and `channel`, but now populates `files` from `repo.filesAt(stable)` where `stable = repo.headCommit("stable")`. Every snapshot is therefore internally inconsistent: `commit`/`channel` identify the requested channel while `files` belongs to the stable channel. Publishing any non-stable channel silently emits stable's file list under the wrong commit/channel. Additionally, the new unconditional `repo.headCommit("stable")` call makes the function fail for any repo/channel where 'stable' does not exist, even when the requested channel is valid.

findings.title: publishSnapshot mixes stable files with requested-channel commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The function resolves `head = repo.headCommit(channel)` and reports it as `commit` (line 16), but now populates `files` from `repo.headCommit("stable")` (lines 14, 18). For any channel other than one that happens to equal stable's tip, the returned Snapshot claims `commit` is the channel's head while `files` are the contents of `stable`. A consumer that trusts the Snapshot invariant 'files are the tree at commit, on channel' will publish/serve the wrong file set — e.g. publishSnapshot(repo, "feature-x") returns feature-x's commit but stable's files. The hardcoded "stable" also ignores the `channel` argument entirely and adds a new failure mode: on a repo with no `stable` ref, `headCommit("stable")` is called and can throw even though only `channel` was ever needed before.

A caller doing `build(prefix, limit=3)` still receives 10 elements, and `build(prefix, limit=20)` also receives 10. The parameter's promised capping behavior (the only reason to pass it) is not implemented, so any caller sizing, indexing, or persisting based on the requested limit gets a wrong-length result with no error.

findings.title: parse_positive_int promises positivity but never validates it
findings.whyItBreaks: The public symbol was renamed to `parse_positive_int`, which promises it parses/validates a positive integer, but the body is still `return int(value)`. `int('-5')` returns -5 with no error, and `int('0')` returns 0, so zero and negative inputs are silently admitted. A caller using the public name as an input-validation gate receives invalid values instead of a rejection (e.g. `parse_positive_int('-5')` -> -5; `charge('-5')` -> -500). The promise and implementation disagree on the result/data the caller receives, so the contract is wrong with or without an in-repo caller.

It accepts 0 and negative values, so a caller trusting the name performs no separate validation. `charge` (line 6) forwards the result straight into money math (`return n * 100`, line 7) and `total_cents` (line 10) sums those, so `charge(-5) == -500` and `total_cents([-5]) == -500` instead of raising. findings.title: parse_positive_int promises validation but accepts zero/negative
findings.whyItBreaks: This PR renames the public carrier from read_int to parse_positive_int, whose name promises that the parsed value is validated as positive. The body is unchanged `return int(value)` (line 2), which accepts 0 and negative integers and performs no sign check. The only caller, charge() at line 6, relies on that promise for its amount and now computes n*100 for a non-positive value, e.g. charge(-5) returns -500 and total_cents([-5]) returns -500 instead of rejecting a non-positive amount. The old name read_int made no validation promise, so this is drift introduced by the rename, not a pre-existing bug.

findings.title: apply_values now mutates caller's DataFrame (defensive copy removed)
findings.whyItBreaks: Base version computed `result = df.copy()` and wrote into `result`, so `df` was left untouched and the modified frame was returned. The head version writes `df.loc[...] = value` and returns the same `df`, so the caller's input object is mutated in place. For a public helper this is a silent semantic change: any caller that reuses its DataFrame after calling apply_values (e.g. passes a shared/global frame, keeps an untouched reference for comparison, or reuses it in a second transform) now observes its data overwritten. This is the explicitly in-scope 'dropped defensive copy / in-place mutation of caller data' class.

findings.title: Restore the defensive copy; apply_values now mutates caller data
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version did `result = df.copy()` and wrote into the copy, so `apply_values` was pure: the caller's frame was untouched and the returned frame was a distinct object. The head version writes `df.loc[df["key"] == key, "value"] = value` directly into the passed-in frame and returns that same object, so every caller that keeps using the original DataFrame after the call (e.g. saving/comparing/reporting it, or calling apply_values more than once on the same frame to build alternative mappings) now sees its input silently overwritten and accumulates mappings across calls. This is an observable, silent semantic change from a non-mutating to an in-place API; no caller signature changed to advertise it, and pandas emits no warning for this direct `.loc` assignment.

findings.title: apply_values now mutates caller's DataFrame in place
findings.whyItBreaks: Base version created `result = df.copy()` and wrote into the copy, so the caller's `df` was never modified and the function was effectively pure. Every caller that still holds a reference to the passed DataFrame now observes its `value` column silently rewritten. No in-repo callers exist (only the definition is present), so the regression surfaces in downstream consumers of this public module-level function; the documented/observed contract of a non-mutating return is broken by this PR.

findings.title: Remove dbg!(items): it moves items and breaks compilation
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!($expr)` expands to `match $expr { tmp => { eprintln!(...); tmp } }`, binding the scrutinee by value, so `dbg!(items)` consumes `items`. `Vec<String>` is not `Copy`, so the unchanged `items.len()` on line 3 is a use-after-move and the crate fails to build with `error[E0382]: use of moved value: 'items'` (value moved at line 2, used at line 3). Independently, shipping an unconditional `dbg!` writes the entire input vector to stderr on every call (diagnostic noise + potential data exposure).

findings.title: Remove `dbg!(items)` — it moves `items`, breaking `items.len()`
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!($val)` expands to `match $val { tmp => { eprintln!(...); tmp } }`, which takes `$val` by value and returns it. Since `items` is an owned `Vec<String>` (non-Copy) and the macro result is discarded, `items` is moved on line 2. Line 3 then reads `items.len()`, which the borrow checker rejects with E0382 "borrow of moved value: `items`", so the crate no longer builds. Even if it compiled, `dbg!` unconditionally dumps the entire input vector to stderr in production.

findings.title: dbg!(items) moves items, breaking items.len() (compile error)

As a secondary effect, the macro unconditionally writes the full contents of `items` to stderr (printable, potentially sensitive data left in a production path).

findings.title: Compute changedPaths against pinned revision, not 'latest'
findings.whyItBreaks: buildChangeset resolves the caller's pinnedTag into `from` and returns it as fromRevision, but now reads the path set with store.readChangedPaths(latest). The Changeset contract (lines 6-9) states fromRevision is the revision changedPaths were computed against and that consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly that revision. `latest` is a different, moving revision, so the returned changedPaths describe a different range than fromRevision: the pinnedTag argument no longer governs the result, and a consumer replaying the paths on fromRevision gets a mismatched (typically empty or HEAD-relative) changeset. The base revision passed `from`, so this is an introduced regression.

findings.title: Compute changedPaths against fromRevision, not "latest"
findings.whyItBreaks: The added `const latest = store.resolve("latest")` is then passed to `store.readChangedPaths(latest)` while `fromRevision` is still set to `from` (the resolved pinnedTag). The `Changeset.fromRevision` doc contract states it is 'Revision the changed paths were computed against' and that 'Consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision.' The body now violates that: changedPaths are computed against "latest" but are labeled/replayed against the pinned revision. The store interface confirms the parameter is a from-revision (`readChangedPaths(fromRevision: string)`), so the two values must match; the change silently returns a changeset whose path set belongs to a different revision than the one consumers apply it to, dropping/adding changes during replay.

findings.title: Compute changedPaths from pinned revision, not 'latest'
findings.whyItBreaks: `fromRevision` is set to `store.resolve(pinnedTag)`, but `changedPaths` is now read via `store.readChangedPaths(latest)` where `latest = store.resolve("latest")`. The Changeset contract explicitly documents fromRevision as "Revision the changed paths were computed against. Consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision" (src/changeset.ts:7-9), and `readChangedPaths(fromRevision)` takes that base as its argument (src/changeset.ts:3). The returned pair is now internally inconsistent: paths computed against `latest` are handed to consumers who replay them on top of the pinned revision. Any tag that is not `latest` (i.e. every pinned tag) therefore yields a changeset computed from the wrong base — the replayed path set is wrong (not the pinned-tag-to-head delta) with no error raised.

findings.title: Charge swallows gateway error and returns nil on failure
findings.whyItBreaks: Charge is an exported function whose `error` return is the only signal callers have for a failed charge. On gw.Submit failure the new code calls log.Printf and falls through to `return nil`, so Charge reports success even though no payment was submitted. Failure and the zero/success value are now indistinguishable: a caller doing `if err := pay.Charge(...); err != nil` will proceed as if the charge succeeded, potentially releasing goods/services without payment. The base version propagated the cause via `fmt.Errorf("charge failed: %w", err)`.

Every caller of this exported function now sees a nil error for a failed charge and cannot distinguish failure from success, so it may mark an order paid, bill, or persist state for a payment that never succeeded. This is the post-change contract of a public API, so it holds even though the repo currently has no in-repo callers.

This defeats the per-tenant contract implied by the still-present tenantId parameter and exposes one tenant's settings to another.

findings.title: Await before in-memory decrement lets concurrent reserves oversell
findings.whyItBreaks: The stock guard (line 16) and the in-memory decrement (line 18) are now separated by `await this.store.save(...)` (line 17). When two callers reserve the last unit concurrently, both read `remaining = 1`, both pass `remaining <= 0`, both call `store.save(sku, 0)` and both return `true`; the Map is ultimately set to 0 and the store persists 0, so two reservations succeed against one unit (lost update / oversell). In the base revision the read-check-set was fully synchronous and therefore atomic in the single-threaded runtime; introducing the await created the window.

findings.title: Await between stock check and decrement allows oversell race
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve() reads `remaining`, checks `remaining <= 0`, then `await this.store.save(...)` yields the event loop before `this.stock.set(...)`. Two concurrent reserve() calls for the same sku both read the same remaining, both pass the check, both persist the same `remaining - 1`, and both resolve true. With stock=1, two callers each reserve one unit: the count is decremented only once (lost update) while two reservations succeed, i.e. the inventory is oversold. Before this change the method was fully synchronous, so get/check/set ran as one atomic turn of the event loop; the added await is what opens the TOCTOU window.

findings.title: Async reserve() races and oversells between read and write
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve() now reads this.stock (line 15), checks remaining <= 0 (line 16), then awaits this.store.save (line 17) before writing this.stock (line 18). The await yields the event loop inside the read-check-write critical section that was previously atomic because the method was synchronous. Two concurrent reserve(sku) calls with stock=1 both read remaining=1, both pass the guard, both persist 0 and both set the map to 0 and return true. Result: two successful reservations from one unit (oversell) and the persisted count is also 0 for two claims. The base version's synchronous reserve() could not interleave.

findings.title: retry() now sleeps 1000x too long after backoff unit change
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() was changed to return milliseconds: `Math.min(30_000, 2 ** attempt * 1000)`. The PR correctly updated its call site in src/net/poll.ts:4 to drop the `* 1000`, but the other existing caller, src/jobs/retry.ts:12, still does `await sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`. So the unit conversion is now applied twice. With the new backoff: attempt 0 returns 1000 (ms), then retry multiplies by 1000 → 1,000,000 ms ≈ 16.7 min; attempt 5 hits the cap 30,000, then ×1000 → 30,000,000 ms ≈ 8.3 hours per retry. Previously these were 1,000 ms and 30,000 ms. Retry-based jobs will appear hung and will blow through any job/request timeout.

findings.title: retry() sleeps backoff(a)*1000 after backoff unit changed to ms
findings.whyItBreaks: This PR changed backoff() from seconds (Math.min(30, 2**attempt)) to milliseconds (Math.min(30_000, 2**attempt*1000)) and updated src/net/poll.ts to pass the result straight to setTimeout. The second caller, src/jobs/retry.ts:12, was not updated and still does `await sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`. With the new ms-returning backoff, that yields 1000x the intended delay: attempt 0 -> 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 min), and the cap becomes 30,000,000 ms (~8.33 hours) instead of the intended 30 s. Every retried async job is effectively stalled for minutes-to-hours, breaking the retry workflow. Before the change both callers multiplied by 1000 and the cap was 30 s, so this is a regression introduced by this diff.

findings.title: Fix retry() delay after backoff() switched units to ms

For the first retry (a=0) that is min(30000, 1000)*1000 = 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 min) vs 1,000 ms before; at a>=5 it caps at 30,000,000 ms (~8.3 h) vs 30,000 ms (30 s) before. Retry-backed jobs now stall for hours, a 1000x user-facing regression. poll.ts:4 was updated to drop the *1000 and stays identical because min(30000, 2**a*1000) == min(30, 2**a)*1000 for all a.

findings.title: Save drops f.Close() error that was previously returned
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version ended with `return f.Close()`, so any error from closing the destination file reached the caller. The new version replaces that with `defer f.Close()` (line 13) plus `return w.Flush()` (line 20); the deferred Close runs after the return value is already fixed to the Flush result, so its error is silently discarded. os.File.Close can fail after a successful buffered Flush (e.g. delayed-allocation/quota/NFS close-time writeback errors), and Save is an exported write path: a caller checking `if err := store.Save(...); err != nil` now receives nil on that failure, conflating a failed close with a durable write. This is exactly the swallow class in TRIGGER D — the signal previously reached the caller (base file: `return f.Close()`), and now reaches nobody.

findings.title: Save drops f.Close() error, returning success on failed close
findings.whyItBreaks: Base version returned the error from f.Close() on the success path (base store/save.go:24), so a close-time failure propagated to the caller. The PR replaces that with `defer f.Close()` (line 13) and `return w.Flush()` (line 20): the deferred Close runs after the return value is already evaluated, so its error is silently discarded. bufio.Writer.Flush only pushes bytes to os.File.Write; the OS/filesystem can still report delayed write-back/quota/NFS/FUSE errors at close, so Save can now return nil for a save that never durably landed. This is an exported API, so every caller is forced to conflate a failed close with a successful save.

findings.title: Save discards os.File.Close error via defer, hiding failed writes
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR, Save returned the result of f.Close() (base line 24), so any error surfaced only on close (delayed writeback / disk-full / EIO on network filesystems) reached the caller. The new `defer f.Close()` at line 13 discards that error, and line 20 only returns w.Flush(). w.Flush() pushes the bufio buffer through f.Write, but writeback errors that the kernel reports on close(2) are now swallowed. A caller that checks the returned error will treat a partially/never-persisted save as success — silent data loss on the store's primary write path. Save is an exported public API, so the broken contract is the defect even with no in-repo callers.

findings.title: Fix inverted TTL check: fresh entries return null, expired entries are served
findings.whyItBreaks: The condition was flipped from `< this.ttlMs` to `> this.ttlMs`. Now an entry whose age is less than ttlMs (still fresh) falls through to `this.entries.delete(key); return null;`, while an entry older than ttlMs (expired) is returned. Every fresh lookup is a miss and is evicted, and stale data is served past its TTL, defeating the entire purpose of TtlCache.

findings.title: Don't splice during forEach: adjacent done jobs survive pruneDone
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.forEach increments its index regardless of element removal. When a done job is spliced at index i, the next element shifts into slot i but the iterator advances to i+1, so that element is never visited. Example: `[done, done, open]` — index 0 (done) is removed, array becomes `[done, open]`, forEach moves to index 1 (open) and stops, leaving a done job in the result. Consecutive done jobs are silently retained, which is the exact set pruneDone is supposed to remove (base used `jobs.filter((job) => !job.done)`).

findings.title: pruneDone now mutates the caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation returned a new array and left the input untouched. The new body calls `jobs.splice(index, 1)` and returns the same reference, so any caller holding the original array sees it suddenly lose elements. Callers that reuse the passed array (e.g. to iterate or re-prune) now observe a partially mutated list they did not opt into.

findings.title: TTL expiry check inverted: fresh entries evicted, stale served
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate now returns entry.value only when the entry is older than ttlMs (Date.now() - storedAt > ttlMs), and when the entry is still fresh it falls through to entries.delete(key) + return null. This inverts the cache: every fresh lookup is a miss and the entry is destroyed, while expired entries are returned as if valid. The subsequent delete/null branch at lines 21-22 is only reachable for entries that should have been returned.

findings.title: pruneDone splices while iterating, skipping adjacent done jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: jobs.splice(index,1) mutates the array that forEach is walking. After removing index i, the next element shifts into index i and forEach advances to i+1, so it is never visited. For input [{done:true},{done:true},{done:false}] the first done is removed, the second shifts to index 0, forEach moves to index 1 and never sees it, so the function returns [{done:true},{done:false}] instead of [{done:false}]. Any run of consecutive done jobs leaves all but the first behind.

findings.title: pruneDone now mutates the caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed implementation returned a fresh array (jobs.filter) and left the input untouched. The new implementation calls jobs.splice(...) on the argument and returns that same reference, so any caller still holding the original array observes its done jobs silently removed. Callers that reuse the original list (e.g. to report or retry) now see mutated data. This aliasing change is independent of the iteration bug and would remain even if the loop were made index-safe.

findings.title: Inverted TTL check serves expired cache entries and evicts fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: `Date.now() - entry.storedAt > this.ttlMs` is true only once the entry is EXPIRED, yet that branch returns `entry.value`. The correct TTL test is the opposite: a fresh entry (age < ttlMs) must be returned. With this change, immediately after `set` the age is ~0, so the condition is false, the fresh entry is deleted, and `get` returns null (100% miss); any time after the TTL elapses the condition becomes true and the stale value is served forever (never evicted, since the else-branch delete only runs while fresh). This fully inverts cache semantics.

findings.title: pruneDone splice-during-forEach skips consecutive done jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Mutating the array with `splice(index, 1)` while `forEach` is iterating shifts every later element down one index, but forEach still advances its index. So the element immediately after any removed job is never visited. Concretely, `pruneDone([{done:true},{done:true},{done:false}])` removes the first entry at index 0, then the loop's next index 1 sees the shifted `{done:false}` and skips the second `{done:true}`, returning `[{done:true},{done:false}]` — a done job survives. (It also now mutates the caller's input array in place instead of returning a new array, unlike the previous `filter`.)

findings.title: Restore empty-array guard in averageAmount to avoid NaN
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` means an empty input computes 0/0. `[].reduce(..., 0)` is 0 and `0 / rows.length` is 0/0 = NaN. Any caller of this exported function that previously received the numeric 0 for an empty set now receives NaN, which silently poisons subsequent sums/averages, fails equality/range comparisons, and serializes to null in JSON. Empty input was an explicitly supported case before this diff.

findings.title: Stop busiest from mutating the caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation sorted a copy (`[...rows].sort(...)`) and left the caller's array untouched. The new body calls `rows.sort(...)` directly, which reorders the caller's array in place as an observable side effect of a read-only-looking query named `busiest`. Callers that hold a `Row[]` and later read it (iteration order, pagination, id/index lookups) now see it reordered by descending amount. This exported helper silently changes its input, a regression from the previous non-mutating contract.

findings.title: Restore empty-input guard: averageAmount now returns NaN
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` guard means an empty input now computes 0 / 0, which is NaN, not 0. Callers that aggregate or display the result get NaN, which propagates through further arithmetic and makes every comparison false (NaN !== NaN), silently corrupting any reporting downstream. This is a behavior change from the function's previous contract for a real input (empty result set).

findings.title: busiest now mutates caller's array with in-place sort
findings.whyItBreaks: `Array.prototype.sort` sorts the receiver in place. The previous implementation copied first (`[...rows].sort(...)`), so the caller's array was left untouched. After this change, any caller that still uses `rows` after calling `busiest` observes it silently reordered by descending amount. Mutating a caller-owned array inside a read-only-looking query helper is an observable side effect and a regression from the prior contract.
