This is a silent behavior regression of an exported function: callers that pass an empty dataset receive NaN, which poisons any downstream sum/average/UI math, whereas before this PR they received a valid `0`. NaN is typed as `number`, so nothing surfaces the change at the type level.

findings.title: busiest now mutates the caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation sorted a shallow copy (`[...rows]`), guaranteeing `busiest(rows)` left `rows` unchanged. The new `rows.sort(...)` sorts the caller's array in place as a side effect. Any caller that relies on the original order (or shares the array with other logic) silently gets its data reordered, producing order-dependent wrong results/bugs that are invisible from the signature.

findings.title: Restore numeric comparator in score sort (lexicographic regression)
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code did `scores.sort((a, b) => b - a)` (numeric descending). The new rankScores() does bare `scores.sort()`, which coerces numbers to strings and orders them lexicographically by UTF-16 code units, then reverse()s. topPlayers() derives its inclusion threshold from this ordering: `cutoff = scores[Math.min(n, scores.length) - 1]` and filters `p.score >= cutoff`. With string ordering the cutoff is wrong, and because the filter preserves original array order before `.slice(0, n)`, a wrong/lower cutoff admits low scorers and can return the wrong players. Concrete substitution: players=[{score:3},{score:100},{score:20}], n=1 → rankScores maps [3,100,20] → sort() → [100,20,3] → reverse → [3,20,100] → cutoff=scores[0]=3 → filter keeps all three → slice(0,1) returns [{score:3}], i.e. the LOWEST scorer instead of {score:100}. The old comparator returned [100].

findings.title: Restore numeric comparator in rankScores; default sort orders scores as strings
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator coerces elements to strings and compares UTF-16 code units. Numbers of different magnitude no longer rank numerically: for players [9, 100, 10], sort() yields [10,100,9], reverse() yields [9,100,10]. With n=1 the cutoff becomes scores[0]=9, filter(score>=9) keeps all three in original order, and slice(0,1) returns the score-9 player instead of the score-100 player. More generally the cutoff is the nth lexicographically-largest value, not the nth numerically-largest, so topPlayers returns a wrong set and formatBoard renders a wrong leaderboard. Before this diff the code used scores.sort((a,b)=>b-a), which was numerically correct.

findings.title: Restore numeric comparator in rankScores (default sort is lexicographic)
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator coerces scores to strings and orders lexicographically; reverse() then only inverts that wrong order. For scores [9, 10, 100], sort() yields [10, 100, 9], reverse() yields [9, 100, 10], so scores[Math.min(n, len)-1] (line 15) is 9 for n=1 instead of 100. The filter `p.score >= cutoff` then admits every player and slice(0,1) returns the first-array player (score 9) rather than the top scorer (100). Any multi-digit/mixed-width score set produces a wrong cutoff and wrong leaderboard; formatBoard (line 19) inherits the wrong ordering. The base revision used scores.sort((a, b) => b - a), which was correct.

findings.title: Restore constant-time comparison in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() previously used hmac.compare_digest, which compares in constant time. The new `signature_of(payload, secret) == given_signature` uses Python's str equality, which short-circuits at the first mismatching character. Because expected and attacker-supplied signatures are compared byte-by-byte with early exit, an attacker who can submit many webhook requests and measure response timing can recover the correct hex digest one character at a time and forge a valid signature, defeating the authentication performed by handle() (line 14). This is CWE-208; the base revision (70a6e6a1) deliberately used the constant-time primitive.

findings.title: Restore constant-time comparison in webhook signature verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: hmac.compare_digest performs a constant-time comparison; the replacement `signature_of(payload, secret) == given_signature` short-circuits on the first differing byte, leaking how many leading hex characters of the expected digest match the attacker-supplied signature. An attacker who can submit webhook requests and measure response timing can recover a valid signature byte-by-byte and bypass the 401 gate in handle() (app/webhook.py:14), which is the sole authorization check before processor(payload) runs. This is a security weakening introduced by this PR (CWE-208/CWE-347), not a style preference.

findings.title: Restore constant-time comparison in webhook signature verify
findings.whyItBreaks: `==` on str short-circuits at the first differing character, so comparison time correlates with the length of the matching prefix of the expected hex digest. An attacker submitting forged signatures can iteratively recover a valid digest byte-by-byte from response-timing differences, defeating the HMAC check that `verify` is supposed to enforce. The previous `hmac.compare_digest` compares in constant time and does not leak the matching prefix.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs ran inside one `with db.transaction():` block, so any failure rolled all three back. Now only `_record_ledger` runs inside the transaction (line 23); `_apply_balances` runs AFTER the transaction has committed (line 24), so the debit (line 10) and credit (line 13) are two independent statements outside any transaction. If the debit succeeds and the credit fails (constraint/DB error, or a process crash between the two), from_acct is debited, to_acct is never credited, and the ledger already records a completed transfer — money is destroyed and the ledger is inconsistent. Any caller that retries after the raised exception inserts a second ledger row and re-applies the debit, double-spending the source account. No external failure/injection is even required for the crash-between-statements case.

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside transfer transaction, breaking atomicity
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR all three writes (ledger INSERT, debit UPDATE, credit UPDATE) ran inside a single `with db.transaction():` block, so any failure rolled the whole transfer back. The refactor commits the ledger INSERT in its own transaction (line 22-23) and then calls `_apply_balances` at line 24 OUTSIDE any transaction. If either UPDATE raises, the process dies, or the second UPDATE fails after the first succeeds, no rollback occurs: the ledger can record a transfer whose balances were never applied, and the debit/credit pair is itself no longer atomic (source debited without destination credited), silently corrupting account balances. The failure is not surfaced so callers cannot detect the divergence.

findings.title: Move balance updates back inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this diff, the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs ran inside one `with db.transaction():` block, so they committed or rolled back together. After the refactor only `_record_ledger` runs inside the transaction; `_apply_balances(db, from_acct, to_acct, cents)` (line 24) executes after the `with` block exits, i.e. after the ledger insert has been committed. If either UPDATE fails (constraint violation, DB error, crash) or the process dies after the ledger commit, the ledger permanently records a transfer whose balances were never applied (or only the debit partially applied), producing a persisted, inconsistent balance/ledger state. The `cents <= 0` guard and error propagation are unchanged; the defect is purely the lost transaction boundary.

findings.title: billingDay regressed from UTC to server-local date (off-by-one day)
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation derived the string from at.getUTCFullYear()/getUTCMonth()/getUTCDate(), making the billing day a timezone-stable UTC date. The new body uses at.getFullYear()/at.getMonth()/at.getDate(), which resolve in the host's local timezone. For any runtime whose TZ is not UTC (e.g. a server in UTC+8), a timestamp late in the UTC day still returns the previous UTC date, and an early-UTC timestamp returns the next date. Because sameBillingDay() is implemented entirely in terms of billingDay(), both functions now classify ledger events into the wrong billing day, shifting day-boundary logic (aggregation, cutoffs, daily billing totals) by one day across timezones. No surrounding code compensated for the timezone switch, and no timezone is pinned in the repo.

findings.title: billingDay now computes local-time date instead of UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The old body read getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, so billingDay was deterministic and timezone-independent. The new line 4 reads getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, so the returned 'YYYY-MM-DD' now depends on the machine's local timezone (and the TZ env var at runtime). Any Date near a local midnight maps to a different calendar day: e.g. 2024-03-01T01:00:00Z on a server at UTC-08:00 previously yielded '2024-03-01' and now yields '2024-02-29'. The same Date therefore classifies differently across servers/regions/CI, shifting billing-day buckets and boundary logic. Because sameBillingDay (line 8) delegates to billingDay, the equality contract also changes: two instants in the same UTC day can now compare unequal (and vice versa) depending on where the code runs.

findings.title: billingDay switched from UTC to local time, breaking determinism
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, so billingDay produced a stable UTC calendar day independent of the host timezone. The new line reads local-time accessors (getFullYear/getMonth/getDate). For any instant near local midnight the returned day now differs from the previous UTC value, and the SAME instant yields different billing days on hosts with different TZ (e.g. UTC vs America/Los_Angeles) or after a deploy/host TZ change. Because sameBillingDay (day.ts:8) compares these strings, usage/period attribution can flip to the adjacent day, i.e. mis-billing/mis-classification.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenant, causing cross-tenant profile leak
findings.whyItBreaks: The module-level `memo` (src/profile.ts:7) is shared across every tenant. Previously the key was `${tenant}:${account}`, so a lookup was scoped by tenant. After changing the key to `account`, `readProfile(tenantA, "acct")` populates `memo` under `"acct"`, and a later `readProfile(tenantB, "acct")` hits that same entry at line 15 and returns tenantA's cached `Profile` (including its `tenant` and `displayName`) without ever calling `fetchProfile`. Whenever two tenants share an account identifier the second tenant receives the first tenant's profile data — a cross-tenant disclosure and a wrong-result regression, not just a stale cache.

findings.title: Cache key dropped tenant, leaking cross-tenant profiles
findings.whyItBreaks: The module-level `memo` Map is shared across all tenants. Changing the key from `${tenant}:${account}` to `account` means a call `readProfile('tenantA','alice',...)` stores under key 'alice', and a later `readProfile('tenantB','alice',...)` hits `memo.get('alice')`, returns the cached Profile whose `tenant` is 'tenantA', and never calls `fetchProfile('tenantB','alice')`. Any consumer that trusts `profile.tenant`/`profile.displayName` now receives another tenant's identity while believing it is tenant B's — a tenant-isolation/authorization break, and worse, a poisoned cache persists for the process lifetime.

findings.title: Restore tenant to profile cache key to prevent cross-tenant collision
findings.whyItBreaks: `memo` is a module-level Map (src/profile.ts:7) and the key is now just `account` (src/profile.ts:14). The function signature takes both tenant and account and `fetchProfile(tenant, account)` is tenant-scoped, and the returned `Profile` explicitly carries its `tenant` field (src/profile.ts:1-5, 17). Since account identifiers are only unique within a tenant, `readProfile('tenantA','alice', fetchA)` stores under key 'alice', and a later `readProfile('tenantB','alice', fetchB)` hits `if (cached) return cached` (src/profile.ts:16) and returns tenantA's Profile (including tenant:'tenantA', displayName belonging to tenantA) without ever calling fetchB. Same-account users across tenants receive each other's profile data — a cross-tenant data-isolation regression.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and returns empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR, load() threw `missing: ${key}` when the key was absent (base src/store.ts:3). The new catch-all at src/store.ts:6-8 catches that same error and returns "", discarding the failure signal. Because the store is Map<string,string>, a present key may itself hold "" — so every caller now conflates 'key not found' with 'key found and empty'. The in-repo consumer loadAll (src/store.ts:12) maps over keys and will silently emit "" for missing keys instead of surfacing the error, and any external caller relying on the throw for validation/persistence decisions is similarly forced to treat failure as a real value.

findings.title: Do not swallow load's missing-key error by returning empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this diff load() threw Error(`missing: ${key}`) when the key was absent, giving callers a hard, distinguishable failure. The new bare `catch { return ""; }` (lines 6-7) discards that signal and substitutes a legitimate-looking value: a caller can no longer tell a missing key from a genuinely stored empty string. The in-repo caller loadAll (src/store.ts:12) is directly affected: previously `keys.map((k) => load(k, store))` aborted the whole batch by propagating the error; now it returns a same-length array with "" in every missing slot, so position-indexed consumers proceed as though the value were present. Because load is exported, the unusable failure/empty conflation is itself a public contract defect even outside this repo.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and returns empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, load() threw `missing: ${key}` when the key was absent, so a missing entry was a distinct, propagating failure. The new catch-all maps that error (and any error thrown by store.get, e.g. a null store) to "", the same value a caller gets when the key legitimately exists with an empty-string value. The exported load() and its wrapper loadAll() therefore destroy the failure signal: callers can no longer tell 'not found / broken store' from 'found empty value' and will treat a missing entry as a real empty value (e.g. render/persist/compute on ""). This is a public contract defect that ships now, independent of whether the repo has an internal caller.

findings.title: Renaming Config.timeoutMs to timeout silently disables the retry deadline
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported field `timeoutMs` is renamed to `timeout` with no compatibility shim. An existing caller that still supplies `timeoutMs` (JS callers, `as Config` casts, or callers that cross an untyped boundary) leaves `config.timeout === undefined`. At line 8 `Date.now() + undefined` evaluates to `NaN`, and the guard `if (Date.now() > deadline) return;` at line 10 compares against NaN, which is always false. The timeout check therefore never fires and `retry` runs all `maxAttempts` regardless of the configured timeout — a silent behavioral regression, not a compile-time error. The same value/guard pair is duplicated at lines 21/23 in retryBackground.

findings.title: retryBackground swallows every failure and returns void with no signal
findings.whyItBreaks: The new public `retryBackground` catches all errors and `continue`s, then returns `void` once the loop exhausts. A caller cannot distinguish 'fn eventually succeeded' from 'every attempt failed' (or from 'the retries/deadline budget ran out before any attempt'). Since the failure is neither rethrown, returned, nor logged, this exported API forces every caller to conflate failure with success — the defect is in the contract itself even with no in-repo callers (TRIGGER D: discarded failure signal).

findings.title: New required Config.retries diverges from retry's maxAttempts and can no-op silently
findings.whyItBreaks: Adding a required `retries` field breaks every existing `Config` object literal (including callers of the unchanged `retry`, which never reads `retries`). Worse, the two functions use different attempt fields: `retry` loops on `maxAttempts` (line 9) while `retryBackground` loops on `retries` (line 22), so one `Config` yields different attempt counts depending on the callee. At runtime, if `retries` is absent (old config object, cast, JS caller), `i < config.retries` is `0 < undefined` → false, the loop body never executes, `fn` is never called, and the function returns `void` as if it had succeeded — a silent no-op rather than a validation error.

findings.title: Renaming timeoutMs to timeout breaks callers and disables deadline
findings.whyItBreaks: Config is exported and its field `timeoutMs` was removed/renamed to `timeout`, while a new required `retries` field was added. TypeScript consumers passing `{maxAttempts, timeoutMs}` now fail to compile (missing `timeout`/`retries`, excess `timeoutMs`), and untyped/JS consumers silently get `config.timeout === undefined`; then `deadline = Date.now() + config.timeout` (src/retry.ts:8 and :21) is `NaN`, so the guard `Date.now() > deadline` (src/retry.ts:10 and :23) is always false and the configured timeout is silently disabled — every attempt runs regardless of the deadline.

findings.title: retries=0 makes retryBackground skip fn and return silently
findings.whyItBreaks: The loop bound is `i < config.retries`. `retries` conventionally counts retries after the first attempt, so `retries: 0` means 'do not retry' but must still invoke fn once. Here the loop body never executes, fn is never called, and the `void` function returns as if it succeeded, so the caller cannot distinguish 'never attempted' from 'succeeded'. The same silent no-op occurs when a config built for `retry` (which populates `maxAttempts`, not `retries`) is passed in, since `retries` is then undefined.

findings.title: retryBackground swallows all failures with no signal
findings.whyItBreaks: The newly added `catch { continue; }` discards every exception thrown by fn; when all attempts fail the function returns void with no error, no return value, and no log. Callers cannot distinguish a successful attempt from total failure, so a failed background operation is indistinguishable from success. This is an exported public swallow site, so the API contract itself forces every caller to conflate failure with a real value.

findings.title: Breaking public Config rename + required retries field
findings.whyItBreaks: Config is an exported public carrier consumed by the exported retry(). The prior field timeoutMs is removed/renamed to timeout and a new required field retries is added. Every existing caller that constructs { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } now fails TypeScript compilation (excess property timeoutMs, missing timeout and retries), and even a migrated caller must supply retries, which retry() never reads. Additionally the 'Ms' unit is dropped: lines 8/21 still add config.timeout to Date.now(), so a migrated caller following the old millisecond contract can pass seconds and get a 1000x-too-long deadline.

findings.title: New exported retryBackground swallows all errors, returns void
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground catches every error and continues, then falls off the end returning void. No error is logged, rethrown, or encoded in a return value, so a caller cannot distinguish 'fn eventually succeeded' from 'every attempt failed'. A caller will treat a total failure as success and proceed (persist, report success, or skip compensating action). Although retry() has the same catch shape, this is a newly added exported path, so the unusable contract itself ships now.

findings.title: Guard value.length for the newly allowed number type
findings.whyItBreaks: This same diff widens `value` to `string | number` (line 2), but line 6 computes `value.length`. For a numeric value JS evaluates `(42).length` to `undefined`, so the template literal produces `len=undefined` and the input renders that instead of a real length. TypeScript also rejects `.length` on `string | number` (TS2339), so the numeric case the widened type advertises is broken at both runtime and build time.

findings.title: Restore defaultValue as value; length label replaced it
findings.whyItBreaks: The input previously initialized with the caller's `value` (`defaultValue={value}`); it now initializes with the derived `label`. The exported component still advertises a `value` prop, so any consumer passing a value gets an input whose initial content is `len=<n>` instead of the value — a user-visible regression that discards the prop the interface promises to render.

findings.title: Field renders length string instead of the value
findings.whyItBreaks: Base behavior initialized the input with the caller's value (`<input defaultValue={value} />`). The head instead computes `const label = `len=${value.length}`` and passes `defaultValue={label}`, so the controlled default is now a metadata string like `len=3`, not the value. Every consumer that relies on `Field` to display/preserve its `value` gets the wrong field content, even for the original `string` case that previously worked.

findings.title: string|number prop dereferenced with .length
findings.whyItBreaks: The public `FieldProps.value` contract was widened from `string` to `string | number`, promising callers that numbers are valid. The body then reads `value.length` (line 6). `number` has no `length` property, so this is a TypeScript compile error (`Property 'length' does not exist on type 'string | number'`) and, if transpiled without type-checking, evaluates to `undefined`, producing `len=undefined`. The promised contract (numbers accepted) is not implemented by the body.

findings.title: value.length is invalid on string | number (undefined for numbers)
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps.value was widened to string | number (line 2) but the body reads value.length (line 6). A number has no length, so for numeric callers label becomes `len=undefined` and the input renders that; the widened exported contract promises number support the body does not implement. TypeScript also rejects the access: 'Property length does not exist on type number' (TS2339), so the project typecheck/build fails while base compiled.

findings.title: Input no longer renders the value, only a length label
findings.whyItBreaks: Base rendered `<input defaultValue={value} />`; the head renders `defaultValue={label}` where label is `len=${value.length}`. Every existing string caller (e.g. value="abc") now gets an input whose default value is the string "len=3" instead of "abc", a user-visible regression in the exported Field component.

findings.title: Do not echo deployment secret to workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The new step puts `${{ secrets.TOKEN }}` into the step environment and then runs `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, printing the deployment credential into the workflow run log. The log for a `push`-triggered run is retained on the Actions tab and downloadable by anyone with read access to the repo (and by any later workflow/artifact consumer). GitHub log masking is best-effort, not a confidentiality guarantee, so the token value can end up persisted in plaintext. Secrets must never be written to output.

findings.title: Do not echo the TOKEN secret into workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The new step expands `secrets.TOKEN` into a shell command that prints it (`echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`). The value is written to the Actions run log, which is retained and viewable by anyone with repository/actions read access. GitHub's automatic secret masking is best-effort only and does not make printing a secret safe (masking can be defeated by log transforms, multi-line/special-character values, or log exports), so this turns a protected credential into a potential disclosure.

findings.title: Do not echo secrets.TOKEN into CI logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step exports `TOKEN: ${{ secrets.TOKEN }}` and interpolates it into `run: echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, writing the deploy token into the workflow run log. GitHub's automatic secret masking is best-effort and matches only exact registered values; it is bypassed by value transformations/splitting and is not a substitute for not printing the secret. Anyone who can read Actions logs (collaborators, log exports, or a compromised token with actions:read) can recover the token and reuse it for unauthorized deploys. Printing a secret is never needed for a deploy check.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git() to avoid ENOBUFS on large diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: Dropping the explicit maxBuffer lets spawnSync fall back to Node's default of 1024*1024 bytes. git() is used to read the entire PR patch (`git diff mergeBase headSha`, line 140) and the full changed-file list (`git diff --name-only`, line 57). For any PR whose diff output exceeds 1 MiB (lockfiles, generated bundles, large vendored files), spawnSync aborts the child with ENOBUFS, leaving res.status === null; the guard `res.status !== 0` (line 38) is then true, git() throws, and runGithub's catch (lines 182-194) posts a failure check ('Needlefish: review failed') and sets exitCode 1. This worked before up to 64 MiB, so it is a user-facing regression for large PRs. Verified locally: default maxBuffer yields error.code === 'ENOBUFS' with status null and stdout truncated at ~1.06 MiB.

findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer: large diffs now fail review
findings.whyItBreaks: The git() helper previously set maxBuffer to 64 MiB; the new call omits it, so spawnSync falls back to Node's default (~1 MiB). git() is used for the full patch at line 140 (`git diff mergeBase headSha`), which routinely exceeds 1 MiB on large PRs. On overflow spawnSync terminates the child, sets status=null and error=ENOBUFS (verified: status=null, error=ENOBUFS, stdout capped). Line 38 (`res.status !== 0`) is true, so git() throws `git diff ... failed: ` (ENOBUFS is not surfaced and stderr is empty). runGithub's catch at 182-193 then posts a failure check and sets exitCode=1 — the review never runs. The gh()/ghText() helpers (lines 19, 29) still keep 64 MiB, confirming the removal was accidental.

findings.title: Restore git maxBuffer; 1 MiB default kills large PR diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: The 64 MiB maxBuffer was removed from git(), leaving Node's child_process default of 1024*1024 bytes. git() is used to materialize the whole PR patch at line 140: `const patch = git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha], cwd);`. Any PR whose diff exceeds 1 MiB makes spawnSync terminate the child with ENOBUFS (status null), so the guard at line 38 trips and line 39 throws `git diff ... failed:`; on some Node versions the patch is silently truncated instead. Either way a real, common PR size converts a successful review into a hard failure or an incomplete patch. gh()/ghText() kept their 64 MiB cap, so only the git path regressed.

findings.title: bundle.baseSha no longer matches the patch's merge-base
findings.whyItBreaks: In the same function, `patch` (line 140) and `changedFiles` (line 141 via changedFileSet) are both computed against `mergeBase = git(["merge-base", baseSha, headSha])` (line 139). The bundle now advertises `baseSha:` (shorthand for the raw `baseSha` from PR_BASE_SHA / merge-base origin/main HEAD, line 138) instead of `mergeBase`. On the live Actions path baseSha is the base-branch tip; whenever the base branch has advanced past the branch point (ordinary), baseSha != mergeBase, so the emitted Bundle claims a base revision that does not correspond to the patch it carries. A consumer that re-diffs baseSha..headSha or reports baseSha (e.g. review at line 177) then includes unrelated base-branch changes and mis-attributes lines.

findings.title: Restore explicit -s read-only for codex exec subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed CLI flag was a defense-in-depth guarantee, not a redundancy. Codex merges configuration as built-in defaults < ~/.codex/config.toml < project .codex/config.toml < profile < CLI flags (see the config layering docs), so a CLI `-s read-only` overrode any permissive `sandbox_mode`. With the flag gone, `codex exec` now inherits whatever `sandbox_mode` is configured. Because `spawnSync` runs with `cwd: opts.repoPath` (line 23-24) and Codex loads project config from `.codex/config.toml` in that working root, a repo under review can ship a config that raises the sandbox to `workspace-write`/`danger-full-access`; a user's global config can do the same. The model then gets file-write and/or networked command execution while processing the untrusted prompt/diff that this review agent exists to ingest. The current Codex release happens to default `codex exec` to read-only, but that is now an implicit, version/user-config-dependent default rather than an enforced one.

findings.title: Restore forced read-only sandbox for codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the explicit `-s read-only` CLI override makes codex exec resolve its sandbox from the local environment instead of a forced policy. In codex, `ConfigToml::derive_sandbox_policy` resolves `sandbox_mode_override` (the `-s` flag) > `--profile` > config.toml `sandbox_mode` > trusted-project (which maps to WorkspaceWrite) > default. With the flag present, every run against the repo under review was unconditionally read-only. Without it, a user's `~/.codex/config.toml` (`sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"|"danger-full-access"`) or a `[projects."<repo>"] trust_level = "trusted"` entry makes the model writable in `cwd: opts.repoPath` (line 24). `codex exec` also hard-codes `approval_policy = AskForApproval::Never`, so there is no interactive approval backstop. Because the prompt is built from untrusted PR content, a malicious PR can prompt-inject the model into modifying the local checkout or running write commands.

findings.title: Restore `-s read-only` sandbox on runCodex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: `runCodex` spawns `codex exec` with cwd = the repo under review and passes the review prompt (attacker-controlled diff/source) on stdin. The removed `-s read-only` was the only thing guaranteeing the Codex agent's model-generated shell commands could not write. With the flag gone, sandbox selection falls back to config/trust: in codex-cli 0.154.0 the default built-in permission profile is `:workspace` (workspace-write) whenever the project is trusted or untrusted (codex-rs/core/src/config/permissions.rs:48-59), and any user `sandbox_mode`/`default_permissions` (up to danger-full-access) is now honored instead of being overridden. A prompt-injected review target can therefore cause the agent to write/delete/modify files in the repository under review, which the read-only reviewer must never do.

findings.title: Restore merge-base / PR head in patch computation
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch is now `git diff baseSha HEAD` instead of `git diff $(git merge-base baseSha headSha) headSha`. Two concrete regressions. (1) Two-dot diff vs merge-base: when PR_BASE_SHA is the base branch tip (its name and the Actions-only GITHUB_REPOSITORY guard at line 134 imply GitHub Actions, where PR_BASE_SHA is normally `github.event.pull_request.base.sha`) and the PR branch forked from an older commit, `git diff baseSha HEAD` also renders all of the base branch's intervening commits as additions/deletions. The reviewer then analyzes unrelated base changes as part of the PR, producing false findings and mis-classified changedFiles (line 140). (2) `headSha` (line 137, from PR_HEAD_SHA) is no longer used for the diff even though it is the commit the review is attached to (commit_id at line 85, head_sha at line 124, posted at lines 178-179). Under the default `pull_request` checkout (refs/pull/N/merge) HEAD is the merge commit and differs from PR_HEAD_SHA, so patch line numbers do not correspond to the commit they are posted on; GitHub can reject the review (422) and the catch-all at lines 96-108 then silently downgrades to a body-only review, dropping every inline comment.

findings.title: Restore merge-base before diffing base to head
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior code derived `mergeBase = git merge-base(baseSha, headSha)` and diffed `mergeBase..headSha`. The new code diffs `baseSha` directly against HEAD, i.e. a two-dot diff. `baseSha` comes from `PR_BASE_SHA` (@:138), which in standard Actions is the base-branch tip (`github.event.pull_request.base.sha`), not an ancestor of HEAD. When the base branch has advanced since the PR diverged, `git diff baseSha HEAD` includes the inverse of every commit that landed on base after divergence, and `changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha)` (@:57) classifies those unrelated files as PR changes. `changedPaths` gates `inlineComments` (@:63, @:81) and `patch`/`changedFiles` feed the reviewer bundle (@:139-140, @:166-167), so the bot can emit findings about code not in the PR and attempt inline comments on files outside the PR diff.

findings.title: Restore merge-base so PR diff excludes base-branch changes
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed line anchored the diff at the common ancestor of base and head (`git merge-base baseSha headSha`), i.e. the three-dot PR diff GitHub displays. The new code diffs the base commit directly against the checked-out `HEAD`. When `PR_BASE_SHA` is the base-branch tip rather than an ancestor of the PR head (the base code explicitly computed merge-base(baseSha, headSha), so it did not assume baseSha was an ancestor) and `HEAD` is the PR head, `git diff baseSha HEAD` is a two-dot diff: every commit merged to the base branch after this PR forked appears in the patch with its additions shown as deletions. The polluted patch is handed to `review()` (line 176) and `changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha)` (line 140) feeds `changedPaths` (line 141). `inlineComments()` gates inline comments on `changedPaths.has(f.file)` (line 63); a comment on a file outside the PR diff is rejected by the GitHub review API, and the catch at lines 91-96 then re-posts the review with no inline comments, silently dropping all legitimate inline findings. The patch target also changed from the advertised `headSha` to local `HEAD`, so the reviewed content can diverge from the `commit_id` posted at line 178.

findings.title: Restore function replacers to stop $ patterns corrupting prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace with a *string* replacement interprets `$$`, `$&`, `` $` ``, `$'`, `$n`, `$<name>` as substitution patterns; with a *function* replacement the return value is inserted verbatim. Base code used `() => JSON.stringify(bundle, null, 2)` (line 25), `() => JSON.stringify(candidate, null, 2)`, and `() => bundle.patch`. Head passes the values directly. `bundle.patch` is arbitrary PR diff text, and `bundle` (line 25) embeds that patch, so any `$&` in the diff is replaced by the literal match `{{PATCH}}`, `` $` `` injects the whole text before the placeholder (the critic template prefix), `$'` injects everything after it (the template suffix), and `$$` collapses to `$`. The critic (and reviewer) therefore receives a duplicated/corrupted template with patch content lost or duplicated, producing a wrong review.

findings.title: Restore function replacers to stop `$` pattern expansion
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace interprets `$&`, `` $` ``, `$'`, `$$`, `$<name>` in a STRING replacement, but inserts a function's return literally. The pre-change code passed `() => ...` precisely to make bundle/patch JSON literal. Removing the callback re-enables substitution: e.g. a reviewed file containing `text.replace(/a/g, "$&")` makes `.replace("{{PATCH}}", bundle.patch)` inject the matched `{{PATCH}}` token back into the patch (verified with node), and `$'` injects *all* remaining prompt text. The critic then receives a silently corrupted `{{PATCH}}`/`{{FINDINGS}}`/`{{BUNDLE}}` payload, so pruning runs on wrong data while no error is raised.

findings.title: Restore function replacers so `$` in JSON/patch isn't expanded
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace treats the replacement as a string and expands `$$`, `$&`, `` $` ``, `$'`, and `$n`/`$<name>` patterns when the second argument is not a function. The diff removes the `() =>` wrapper at line 25 (`JSON.stringify(bundle,null,2)`), line 32 (`JSON.stringify(candidate,null,2)`), and line 33 (`bundle.patch`). The payloads are arbitrary: `bundle.patch` is a raw diff and the bundle/candidate JSON embeds repository source, so any `$&` becomes the literal sentinel (`{{PATCH}}`/`{{BUNDLE}}`/`{{FINDINGS}}`), `` $` `` and `$'` inject the surrounding prompt text, and `$$` collapses to `$`. The result is a silently corrupted review/critic prompt (malformed JSON, duplicated prompt text, or a missing/renamed sentinel) that is passed to runCodex at lines 28/34; extractJson can then throw or the model can review wrong text. The removed callback form was the defensive idiom that returns the payload verbatim, so this is a behavioral regression, not a no-op simplification.

findings.title: Restore commit_id pin in postReview fallback path
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch fallback that re-posts a review when the primary `--input -` call fails no longer sends `commit_id=${headSha}` (only the primary JSON payload at line 89 still does). Per the GitHub create-review API, an omitted commit_id defaults to the PR's most recent commit, so the fallback attaches the review body/event to whatever the PR head is at POST time rather than the `headSha` that was actually diffed (`git diff mergeBase headSha`, line 144). Meanwhile postCheck still pins `head_sha: headSha` (line 128). If the PR head advanced during the run, a `REQUEST_CHANGES`/`COMMENT` review describing the reviewed revision is silently recorded against a commit the agent never analyzed, and the review and its check-run disagree.

findings.title: Restore commit_id in fallback review request
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch fallback that re-posts the review when the primary JSON `--input -` call fails no longer sends `commit_id`. GitHub's Create a review endpoint documents that when `commit_id` is omitted it "Defaults to the most recent commit in the pull request". So if the PR head advanced past the reviewed `headSha` (e.g. `PR_HEAD_SHA` was set when the workflow started and a commit landed before/while the review ran, or the primary call failed transiently and the fallback runs later), the fallback records the review against a commit that was never reviewed. The primary path still pins `commit_id: headSha` at line 89, so the two paths now disagree, and `postCheck` still targets `headSha` at line 184, leaving the review and check-run associated with different commits.

findings.title: Restore strict validation in normalizeFinding
findings.whyItBreaks: The rewrite deletes every guard that rejected malformed input and substitutes a default for each failure: invalid/missing severity -> 'P1' (line 98), invalid/missing category -> 'bug' (line 100-102), missing file -> '' (line 103), empty title -> 'Untitled finding' (line 99), empty whyItBreaks/suggestedFix -> '' (line 107-108), and lineStart/lineEnd -> Number(raw.lineStart ?? 0) which can be 0 or NaN (line 104-105). normalizeReview no longer accepts/uses strict=false; it maps every element through the now-never-throwing normalizeFinding (line 131), whereas the base dropped malformed findings in the non-strict branch and threw in the strict branch. Result: a null/empty/garbage model response becomes a plausible-looking P1 'bug' finding on file '' at line 0/NaN instead of failing or being dropped, and the caller cannot tell failure from a legitimate value. (The removed '!raw || typeof raw !== object' guard also means a null element now throws an uncaught TypeError from raw.severity rather than the controlled error.)

findings.title: Malformed findings are silently coerced, not rejected
findings.whyItBreaks: The old normalizeFinding threw on every invalid field (missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, unknown severity/category, non-finite or non-positive lineStart/lineEnd), and normalizeReview either propagated that error (strict=true default) or caught and filtered the bad element (strict=false). The new normalizeFinding never throws: `file: String(raw.file ?? "")` yields "", `lineStart: Number(raw.lineStart ?? 0)` yields 0 (or NaN for a non-numeric value such as "abc"), `lineEnd` likewise, `severity` becomes "P1", and `category` becomes "bug". `normalizeReview` lost its `strict` parameter and unconditionally maps every element, so a malformed model response is now presented to callers as a real, plausible finding anchored to an empty file and line 0 (or NaN), with a fabricated P1 severity. This is a failure-to-value downgrade: the caller can no longer tell 'the model emitted garbage' from 'the model emitted a real P1 finding', and will persist/report the fallback as real. It is an exported public API, so the unusable contract is itself the defect regardless of in-repo callers.

findings.title: normalizeFinding swallows validation errors as default findings
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported normalizeFinding previously threw on malformed input (base: missing file L108, missing title L110, missing whyItBreaks L112, missing suggestedFix L114, invalid lineStart L116-118, invalid lineEnd L119-122, invalid severity L100-102, invalid category L103-106). The new body never throws: it coerces severity to "P1", category to "bug", file/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix to "", and lineStart/lineEnd to 0 (L98, L99, L100-102, L103, L104, L105, L107, L108). normalizeReview no longer propagates these failures either — its strict/default-throwing path was deleted and it now unconditionally maps raw.findings through the non-throwing normalizer (L131). Effect: a malformed or hallucinated finding object is persisted/reported as a real, well-formed Finding with file="", lineStart=0, lineEnd=0, title="Untitled finding", empty rationale/fix. Every consumer is forced to conflate "parse failed" with "valid finding", and a finding anchored to no file / line 0 is not actionable review output. (null/undefined raw.inputs also flow through: undefined ?? default yields the same fabricated object rather than the old "not an object" error.)

findings.title: gh pr view loses explicit repo before checkout; PR refs resolve empty
findings.whyItBreaks: This `Resolve PR refs` step runs BEFORE `actions/checkout` (lines 42-46), so on a fresh/ephemeral self-hosted runner `$GITHUB_WORKSPACE` contains no git repository. `gh pr view` without `-R` resolves the target repo from the current directory's git remote; `gh` does NOT consume `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` (verified with gh 2.98.0: with GITHUB_REPOSITORY set and GH_REPO unset it still errors `failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository`). Only the workflow_dispatch path reaches this `else` branch (EVENT_HEAD empty), so that trigger now fails to resolve refs. The error is swallowed: bash `set -e` does not abort because `echo` succeeds, so `head=` and `base=` are written empty. The checkout then uses `ref: ''` (dispatched branch, not the PR head) and the review receives empty `PR_BASE_SHA`/`PR_HEAD_SHA`, so it reviews the wrong commit. On reused self-hosted runners it may appear to work only because a previous job's checkout is still present.

findings.title: Restore repo context for pre-checkout gh pr view
findings.whyItBreaks: The `REPO` env var and `-R "$REPO"` args were deleted, so `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` must infer the repository. This step (`Resolve PR refs`, lines 26-40) runs BEFORE `actions/checkout` (lines 42-46), so on a fresh/self-hosted runner the default cwd `$GITHUB_WORKSPACE` is not a git repository. gh only resolves the repo from `-R`, `GH_REPO`, or a local git remote's origin; it does NOT read the Actions-injected `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` (verified empirically with gh 2.98.0: in an empty dir with `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` set, `gh pr view` fails `fatal: not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git`, while `GH_REPO` gets past resolution). Because the failing substitution is nested inside `echo "head=$(...)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"` and the default `run` shell is `bash -e`, the step still exits 0 (verified `bash -e -c 'echo "head=$(false)"'` prints `head=` and continues), silently writing empty `head=`/`base=`. Only the `workflow_dispatch` path reaches this `else` branch (pull_request sets `EVENT_HEAD`), and there the job then checks out the triggering ref instead of the PR head and runs the review with empty `PR_BASE_SHA`/`PR_HEAD_SHA`.

findings.title: Restore explicit repo for gh pr view in pre-checkout ref step
findings.whyItBreaks: These `gh pr view` calls run in the `Resolve PR refs` step, which is deliberately ordered before `actions/checkout` (checkout at lines 42-46 needs steps.refs.outputs.head). The old code passed `-R "$REPO"` (with `REPO: ${{ github.repository }}`), so gh never had to infer the target repo. Without `-R`, gh falls back to `go-gh/pkg/repository.Current()`, which resolves the repo only from the `GH_REPO` env var or the current directory's git remotes. Before checkout, the runner workspace has no git remote (on a fresh/cleaned self-hosted workspace it is not a git repo at all), and gh does NOT read `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`. So the else-branch (taken by workflow_dispatch, where EVENT_HEAD is empty) fails with 'unable to determine current repository' / 'not a git repository', breaking the manual review trigger entirely. The automatic pull_request path is unaffected because it uses EVENT_HEAD/EVENT_BASE and never reaches these lines.

findings.title: Candidate pass parsed with strict=false silently drops findings
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview's second parameter is `strict` (default true). Passing `false` selects loose mode, where each normalizeFinding() failure is caught and the finding is filtered out (normalize.ts:187-198; test 'normalizeReview drops malformed findings in loose mode'). The base call used the strict default, so a candidate finding missing/empty file, title, whyItBreaks or suggestedFix, with an invalid severity/category, a non-positive lineStart/lineEnd, or confidence < 0.7 on a non-P3 severity, threw 'malformed finding: ...'. With `false`, that finding is removed from candidate.findings before line 35 serializes `candidate` into the critic prompt. The critic is prune-only (prompts/critic.md), so it cannot reintroduce the dropped finding; line 48 returns pruned.findings and line 43 deriveVerdict can therefore compute `pass` for a review whose first pass actually surfaced a real bug. No log, error, or residual risk records the drop, so a failed/malformed candidate is indistinguishable from a legitimately finding-free one. The critic parse on line 38 remains strict, making the two passes inconsistent.

findings.title: Lenient candidate parse silently drops real findings
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview's second parameter is `strict`. With strict=false each finding is run through normalizeFinding inside a try/catch; any throw (e.g. missing whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, non-blocking severity with confidence<0.7, invalid lineStart, bad severity/category) is mapped to null and filtered out (src/shared/normalize.ts:187-198). The old call used the strict default, so a malformed finding raised a loud error. Now the candidate is accepted, the `!candidate.summary || candidate.checked.length === 0` guard on line 30 only inspects summary/checked and does not notice the missing finding, and line 35 serializes the already-pruned candidate into the critic prompt. The critic therefore never sees the finding, and the final `pruned = normalizeReview(extractJson(rawPruned))` on line 38 only returns what the critic emitted. A malformed-but-real finding is lost end-to-end and deriveVerdict can return `pass` instead of `changes_requested`.

findings.title: Candidate findings silently dropped by lenient normalizeReview
findings.whyItBreaks: Passing the second argument `false` selects normalizeReview's lenient mode (signature `normalizeReview(raw: unknown, strict = true)` at src/shared/normalize.ts:181). In lenient mode each finding is run through `normalizeFinding` inside a try/catch that returns `null` on any Error (src/shared/normalize.ts:190-198) and then filters the `null`s out, so a malformed candidate finding is discarded with no error and no log. Previously (strict default) the same malformed finding caused `normalizeFinding` to throw and the whole `review()` call to fail loudly. A real P1/P2 finding with one bad required field (e.g. missing `suggestedFix`, invalid `severity`, non-positive `lineStart`, or a blocking finding at confidence < 0.7) is therefore removed from `candidate` before it is serialized into the critic prompt at src/core/review.ts:35-36; if it was the only finding, the critic receives an empty `findings` array and can return `pass`, yielding a false-green review. The guard immediately after the changed line (src/core/review.ts:30) only checks `candidate.summary` and `candidate.checked`, so it never detects the drop.

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed-review errors as empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: The five explicit validation throws that previously rejected non-object, missing/non-string summary, and missing/non-array findings/checked/residual_risks were removed and replaced with default fallbacks: `raw?.findings` -> [], `raw?.residual_risks` -> [], `raw?.summary ?? ""` -> "", `raw?.checked` -> []. A malformed model/PR review payload (e.g. plain text, an error object, or a schema mismatch) is now indistinguishable from a legitimately empty review: the function returns {summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]} with no error. A caller orchestrating the review can therefore no longer tell 'the review failed to produce parseable output' from 'the review found zero issues', so it may report a passing/empty verdict instead of retrying or surfacing the malformed output. Because `normalizeReview` is an exported public function, the swallow itself is the defect even though this repo currently has no in-repo caller; every eventual consumer is forced to conflate failure with a real value.

findings.title: Stop swallowing malformed review output in normalizeReview

"")` defaults and no logging, so `normalizeReview(null)`, `normalizeReview("garbage")`, or `normalizeReview({findings:"x"})` all now return `{summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}`. Because findings/residual_risks default to empty and every residual `blocks` defaults to `false`, any consumer that derives a verdict from `findings.length` and `residual_risks.blocks` (the natural use of this exported parser) reads a failed/garbage model response as a clean zero-finding review, e.g. pass, with no error signal and no way to tell it apart from a real review that legitimately found nothing.

findings.title: Restore error on malformed review output instead of empty defaults

The new body maps every one of those failures to `summary: ""`, `findings: []`, `checked: []`, `residual_risks: []` and returns normally. `normalizeReview` is exported and its return type `RawReview` cannot represent "failed" vs "empty", so every caller is forced to treat a corrupt/truncated model response as a valid review containing zero findings and no residual risks. In a review/CI pipeline that can convert a malformed response into a silent clean `pass` instead of an error or a needs_human escalation.

The deleted 'Resolve PR refs' step (base lines 26-43) handled exactly this case by running `gh pr view "$PR_NUM" --json headRefOid` and feeding `steps.refs.outputs.head` into checkout. Because the resolve step is gone, lines 45-46 also pass empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA, and line 35's `github.event.pull_request.base.ref || 'main'` silently fetches/uses 'main' instead of the PR's real base. Manual reviews therefore run against the default branch rather than the requested PR's head.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch now reviews default branch, not the requested PR
findings.whyItBreaks: This workflow explicitly supports `workflow_dispatch` with a required `pr_number` input (lines 10-14) and the job condition admits it (line 24). On a `workflow_dispatch` run there is no `github.event.pull_request` payload, so `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` is empty and the checkout at line 29 falls back to `github.ref`, which for a manual run is the selected branch/tag ref (normally the default branch), NOT the PR head. The removed `Resolve PR refs` step previously called `gh pr view "$PR_NUM" --json headRefOid,baseRefOid,baseRef` precisely for this case, and the CLI was fed `steps.refs.outputs.head/base`. Now lines 45-46 set `PR_BASE_SHA`/`PR_HEAD_SHA` to `github.event.pull_request.base.sha`/`.head.sha`, which are empty on manual runs, so the tool receives no PR SHAs at all. Net effect: manual dispatch reviews the default branch's commits/source instead of the requested PR (self-review mode runs the checkout's own `src/`), and the base/head SHAs the CLI is told to use are blank. The `BASE_REF` default of `'main'` (line 35) further hardcodes a branch that may not be this repo's default.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch no longer resolves the PR head/base refs

findings.title: Removed maxBuffer breaks review of diffs over 1 MiB
findings.whyItBreaks: Node's spawnSync default maxBuffer is 1024*1024 bytes (1 MiB) when the option is omitted (https://nodejs.org/api/child_process.html#child_processspawnsynccommand-args-options; analogous real-world failure: https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/issues/956). The changed line removes the previous 1024*1024*64 (64 MiB) allowance from git(). The live path runLocal() calls git(['diff', baseSha, 'HEAD']) at src/adapters/local.ts:100, and the raw patch is exactly the tool's primary input. For a diff between 1 MiB and 64 MiB the child is terminated and truncated, so res.status is non-zero (ENOBUFS) and the helper throws `git diff ... failed:` with empty stderr (res.error, which carries ENOBUFS, is never surfaced), or worse the truncated patch is used if status is 0. Either way a PR that previously reviewed successfully now fails or is reviewed against incomplete content.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer: git diff over 1 MiB now aborts the review
findings.whyItBreaks: The old call set maxBuffer to 64 MiB; the new call omits it, so spawnSync uses Node's default of 1024*1024 bytes. git(['diff', baseSha, 'HEAD']) at src/adapters/local.ts:100 captures the entire unified diff into stdout. When that diff exceeds 1 MiB (large files, lockfiles, generated code — very common), spawnSync terminates the child and sets res.error=ENOBUFS with res.status=null; the git() guard `res.status !== 0` at line 12 then throws `git diff ... failed:` with an empty stderr. Reviews that previously succeeded on large PRs now fail outright (and the error message is misleading).

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git spawnSync to avoid 1 MiB overflow
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64` makes the git spawnSync fall back to Node's default `maxBuffer` of 1024 * 1024 (1 MiB) (`MAX_BUFFER` in lib/child_process.js, passed into native spawn_sync.cc). This helper is used at src/adapters/local.ts:100 for `git diff <baseSha> HEAD`, the full PR patch, which legitimately exceeds 1 MiB for lockfiles, generated SDKs, or vendored trees. Native `IncrementBufferSizeAndCheckOverflow` calls `SetError(UV_ENOBUFS)` and `Kill()` once buffered stdout/stderr passes the cap. In the common case the child is killed and `res.status` is `null`, so line 12 throws `git diff ... failed:` with an empty stderr because the real cause lives in `res.error` (which is never read), aborting the review. If git has already exited 0 when the overflow is observed, `res.status === 0` and the truncated stdout is returned as if successful, so `review()` analyzes an incomplete patch. Before this diff the 64 MiB cap covered these cases; the sibling `gh` helper at lines 33-37 still sets the same 64 MiB cap, confirming the removal is accidental.

findings.title: Review errors now report neutral, letting failed reviews pass

The summary text is unchanged and still asserts "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR.", so the code now contradicts its own contract: an errored review (crash, unparseable gh/git output, review() exception) reports a non-failing conclusion. GitHub treats neutral as a passing state for required status checks, so if the "Needlefish" check is required, a PR whose review never ran becomes mergeable. neutral is also the same conclusion already used for the legitimate needs_human verdict (VERDICT_CONCLUSION at line 53), so callers/branch protection can no longer distinguish "review crashed" from "review completed and wants human attention" — failure is conflated with a real value.

findings.title: Pin review to checked-out SHA, not live PR head

Findings can be attributed to, or inline-commented against, a revision that was never inspected, and the review no longer pins reproducibly to the reviewed tree.

findings.title: Errored review posts neutral check, bypassing the merge gate

GitHub evaluates a check run with conclusion `neutral` as passing for branch-protection required status checks (community discussions "Neutral checks bypass Required status checks"), so a PR whose review threw can satisfy the required check and be merged. This directly contradicts the unchanged summary on line 193, `Review errored and did NOT pass this PR.`, and the intended contract of the tool. It also collides with the legitimate `needs_human` verdict, which maps to "neutral" (VERDICT_CONCLUSION, line 53), so an infrastructure failure becomes indistinguishable from an intentional non-blocking human-decision verdict.

findings.title: Severity normalization removed; lowercase valid severities downgrade to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code computed `const sev = String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` before the membership test, so untrusted/model-formatted values such as "p0", "p1", " p2 " were accepted and normalized. The new code tests `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity)` on the raw value, so exactly those values now fail the guard. Combined with the default changing from "P1" to "P3", a genuine P0 reported as "p0" (previously normalized to "P0") is now silently classified as the lowest severity "P3"; a missing/non-string severity that used to default to "P1" now defaults to "P3" as well. This mis-classifies findings and can hide critical defects, since normalizeFinding is the sole normalizer used by normalizeReview for raw review output.

findings.title: Restore severity normalization and conservative default in normalizeFinding
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code computed `const sev = String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` and tested membership on that normalized string, falling back to `"P1"`. The new code tests `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity as Severity)` on the raw value and falls back to `"P3"`. This is a live path: `normalizeReview(raw: any)` passes parsed model JSON straight into this function at schema.ts:132, and the `as Severity` cast is compile-time only, so non-canonical runtime values are not normalized before the check. Substituting real values: `{severity:"p0"}` → `includes("p0")` is false → `"P3"` (base: `"P0"`); `{severity:" P1 "}` → `"P3"` (base: `"P1"`); `{}` (missing severity) → `"P3"` (base: `"P1"`). Every such finding is silently reclassified to the least severe bucket — a critical P0 emitted in lowercase becomes P3 — and the fallback for invalid/absent severity is fail-open instead of conservative. `normalizeFinding`'s stated job is normalization, which the new body no longer performs.

findings.title: Restore severity normalization: "p1"/padded values now silently become P3
findings.whyItBreaks: The old body computed `const sev = String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` and matched against SEVERITIES, so lower-case or whitespace-padded severities ("p1", " p0 ") were accepted and returned verbatim. The new body compares the raw value with `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity)` — strict === against exactly "P0".."P3" — so any non-canonical casing/whitespace now fails the match and falls through to the default. The default was also changed from "P1" to "P3", the lowest priority. Net effect: a genuine P0/P1 finding emitted as "p0"/"p1" (or "HIGH", etc.) is silently downgraded to P3 instead of being normalized, which can cause serious findings to be dismissed rather than acted on. This matters because the input is untrusted: normalizeFinding is exported and is fed `raw.findings` where `raw: any` (normalizeReview, line 132), i.e. unvalidated model JSON, which is exactly why the removed trim/uppercase defense existed. I verified the substitute: SEVERITIES array is `["P0","P1","P2","P3"]` (line 85), `"p1" !== "P1"`, so `includes` returns false and the fallback "P3" is returned.

findings.title: Restore GitHub token scrubbing before spawning codex
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously the function built a copy of process.env, deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN, and passed that sanitized env to spawnSync. The PR removes both the deletion block and the `env` option. Per Node's child_process contract, omitting `env` makes the child inherit the full parent environment, so the `codex exec` subprocess (an LLM coding agent) now receives any live GitHub credentials present in the runner's environment. The `-s read-only` flag only constrains filesystem writes and does not prevent the child from reading env vars or making network calls, so the token can be read and exfiltrated by the agent or any code it runs. This re-exposes a secret the code deliberately withheld.

The codex child (an AI agent launched as `codex exec`, which can itself run shell/network actions) now inherits the reviewer's GitHub credentials. Any repo content or model/tool behavior able to read `process.env` or exfiltrate it discloses a token with repository access — the exact exposure the deleted lines were written to prevent. This PR removes both the sanitized object and the `env` option, so spawnSync falls back to its documented default of inheriting the full parent environment (Node.js child_process: `env` Default: `process.env`). The codex child — an LLM agent driven by the untrusted prompt/PR content passed via `input` — therefore receives the review bot's GitHub credentials in its environment. Prompt-injected PR content can direct codex to read and exfiltrate those tokens (e.g. via its model/tooling), allowing repository write/comment actions as the bot. findings.title: Removing fork guard runs untrusted PR code on self-hosted runner

This diff deletes that guard, so the `review` job now also runs for `pull_request` events originating from forks. The job checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` (attacker-controlled fork commit, line 23) and then executes it on a persistent `self-hosted` runner (line 18): `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28, runs project/dependency lifecycle scripts) followed by `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34, the PR's own `src/` per the self-review comment at lines 3-5). A malicious fork PR therefore gets arbitrary code execution on the self-hosted host, letting it read runner-local credentials/caches and pivot into whatever network the runner can reach. GitHub downgrades `GITHUB_TOKEN` to read-only for fork PRs, but that does not mitigate runner-local code execution.

The deleted guard was the only thing restricting execution to same-repo heads. Without it, a fork author controls the checked-out code (line 23, `ref: ...head.sha`) and both executed steps: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28) runs PR-controlled dependency lifecycle scripts, and `tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34) executes PR-controlled source directly. That is arbitrary code execution on a persistent self-hosted runner, enabling runner compromise, lateral movement into the runner's network, and theft of any ambient host credentials. GitHub's own guidance is to not run workflows from forks on self-hosted runners for exactly this reason. The guard was the deliberate control; deleting it is a security-control bypass.
