findings.title: Rejecting 0 silently overrides explicit runner kill-timing config
findings.whyItBreaks: readRunnerDurationMs is the parser for NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS (runner-process.ts:3-10). Both are durations where 0 is a meaningful, valid setting: a 0 grace means SIGTERM is followed immediately by SIGKILL, and a 0 give-up means the runner resolves immediately after SIGKILL. setTimeout(fn, 0) is valid, so 0 was legitimately approvable and the original >= 0 deliberately accepted it. Substituting the new value: value="0" -> Number("0")=0 -> predicate `Number.isFinite(parsed) && parsed > 0` @src/shared/runner-process.ts:135 is false -> returns fallbackMs. For NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS that makes RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=5000 instead of 0, so the hardKillTimer at line 124 fires 5s after SIGTERM instead of immediately; for NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS it makes RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=2000 instead of 0, so finish(null,"SIGKILL") at line 123 waits 2s instead of resolving promptly. An explicit user configuration is silently replaced by the default with no error, warning, or doc change.

findings.title: Duration helper now silently discards an explicit 0 value
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing `parsed >= 0` to `parsed > 0` makes Number('0') fail the validity guard and return fallbackMs instead of 0. Both call sites read this helper from env vars that configure kill timing: NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS. Previously an operator could set either to 0 (a legal delay for setTimeout, meaning 'do not wait') to escalate/settle immediately; now that explicit setting is silently overridden by 5000ms and 2000ms respectively. The change also adds no protection, since negative values were already rejected by `>= 0`, so its only observable effect is dropping a previously-supported configuration value. The helper is an exported public API, so the domain narrowing is itself a contract change.

findings.title: Rejecting 0 silently ignores configured runner kill timing
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported helper now treats the string "0" as invalid and substitutes `fallbackMs`. Its only two call sites read operator config: `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS` (lines 3-6, fallback 5000) and `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS` (lines 7-10, fallback 2000), and the results drive the setTimeout delays at lines 124 and 123. Pre-substitution: value="0" -> parsed=0 -> `0 >= 0` true -> returns 0 -> `setTimeout(..., 0)` (escalate immediately). Post-substitution: value="0" -> `0 > 0` false -> returns 5000/2000. So an operator who explicitly set grace=0 (SIGKILL immediately after SIGTERM) or give-up=0 (stop waiting immediately after SIGKILL) silently gets a 5s/2s delay instead; the configured value is discarded with no warning. The base version `parsed >= 0` explicitly admitted 0, so this is a behavior/compat change on a public helper, not just stricter parsing.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so large PRs never skip changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: In reviewLarge, hotspots are sorted and sliced to MAX_HOTSPOTS (6) at line 93. In base, a deleted block immediately after it computed `covered` from the selected hotspots and pushed a `tail-coverage` hotspot containing every changed file not mapped to any selected surface, with the explicit comment 'never silently skip a changed file'. That block is entirely gone from head, so any changed file that (a) the map pass did not assign to a hotspot or (b) landed in a hotspot cut off by the MAX_HOTSPOTS slice is no longer deep-reviewed at all. For a review tool whose core purpose is not missing defects, a changed critical file can now pass with zero deep inspection.

findings.title: Don't discard deep-pass residual risks in reviewLarge
findings.whyItBreaks: The loop at head lines 97-106 now only concatenates `res.findings` and never reads `res.residual_risks` (base line 127 did `residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)`), and `candidateMerged` hardcodes `residual_risks: []` at line 113. Deep passes can return blocking residual risks (RawReview.residual_risks / ResidualRisk.blocks). They are now dropped before the critic prompt and before `deriveVerdict`, so the merged candidate the critic sees contains no residual risk from any deep pass, and the final `residualRisks` can be empty even though deep passes flagged unresolved blocking evidence. reviewSmall still forwards `candidate.residual_risks` (line 60), so this is a large-path-only silent signal loss and the two paths now disagree.

findings.title: Dedup merges findings differing only by whyItBreaks
findings.whyItBreaks: The dedup key dropped the `whyItBreaks` component (base key included `|${norm(f.whyItBreaks).slice(0, 80)}`). Now two distinct findings that share file, lineStart, category, and the same first 60 title characters collapse to a single entry, keeping only the higher-severity one; the other is silently dropped. Since dedup runs over findings merged from all hotspots, two hotspot passes reporting different defects at the same line under the same short title can lose one.

findings.title: Restore changed-file coverage backstop in reviewLarge
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge keeps only the top MAX_HOTSPOTS=6 hotspots (line 93). The deleted block built `covered` from the selected hotspots and appended a tail hotspot for every changedFile not covered by one, guaranteeing each changed file gets a deep pass. After removal, any file assigned to a hotspot dropped by slice(0,6) - or omitted by the map pass - is never sent to a deep pass, and nothing records the gap: `checked` only lists the reviewed hotspots and residual_risks is empty. A large PR can therefore return a verdict (even pass) while changed files were never inspected.

findings.title: Keep per-hotspot failure isolation in reviewLarge
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted try/catch wrapped `normalizeReview(extractJson(runCodex(deepPrompt, ...)))` and, on failure, recorded a `[name] DEEP PASS FAILED` line plus a `{blocks:true}` residual and continued with the remaining hotspots. Now any throw from runCodex/extractJson/normalizeReview for one hotspot propagates out of the for-loop and rejects the entire reviewLarge call, discarding every finding already collected from earlier hotspots and producing no blocking residual at all.

findings.title: Propagate deep-pass residual risks to the critic/verdict
findings.whyItBreaks: candidateMerged.residual_risks is now hardcoded to [] and `res.residual_risks` is no longer collected. deriveVerdict (line 122) only consumes the critic's residual_risks, and the critic only receives candidateMerged, so a `blocks:true` residual emitted by a deep pass can no longer reach the final verdict. A review that should be blocked can be reported as passing.

findings.title: Restore tail-coverage backstop for unreviewed changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge deep-reviews only the hotspots returned by the map pass after slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS=6). The PR deletes the backstop that pushed every changed file NOT assigned to a selected hotspot into a tail-coverage hotspot. Now any changed file the map model omits (or that sits in hotspots beyond the top 6) is never deep-reviewed, and nothing records the gap (residual_risks is empty), so the result can be a clean PASS while a changed file was never examined. This directly contradicts the removed comment's guarantee that a changed file is never silently skipped.

findings.title: Preserve deep-pass failure containment and residual risks
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR removes the per-hotspot try/catch and the residuals accumulator and hardcodes candidateMerged.residual_risks = []. (1) A failed or malformed deep pass now throws out of reviewLarge, aborting the whole large review and discarding every finding already collected from earlier hotspots, instead of being recorded as a blocks:true residual and continuing. (2) Each successful pass's res.residual_risks (which may include blocks:true) are discarded before the critic. deriveVerdict (src/core/verdict.ts) turns any residual risk with blocks:true into 'needs_human', and only sees pruned.residual_risks, so once deep residuals are replaced with [] the critic can no longer carry a blocking risk forward and the verdict can become 'pass'.

findings.title: Restore {{BASE}}/{{HEAD}} substitution for critic prompt
findings.whyItBreaks: prompts/critic.md still contains `# Refs` with `BASE: {{BASE}}` / `HEAD: {{HEAD}}` and instructs the critic to re-check findings via `git diff <base>..<head>`. reviewSmall (head line 61) and reviewLarge (head line 117) no longer replace these tokens, so the critic receives literal `{{BASE}}`/`{{HEAD}}` text and loses the SHAs needed to open the diff and prune findings, defeating the adversarial pruning step.

findings.title: Restore {{FOCUS}} substitution/focus for large reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: The base deep-prompt chain substituted the template placeholder with `.replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)")` (base src/core/review.ts:122); prompts/deep.md:96 is `Focus: {{FOCUS}} (if not "(none)", prioritize findings in that area)`, so this replacement was the only thing delivering the user's `--focus` to a deep pass. The head removes it, so every deep review of a large PR now sends the literal token `{{FOCUS}}` to the model and no focus guidance. The same hunk also removes `focus`/`deep` from `mapBundle` (head:83-89), so prompts/map.md:37 ("If a `focus` field is set (not null), rank matching surfaces higher") can never trigger for large PRs. reviewSmall still serializes the entire bundle via JSON.stringify at head:52-55, and isLarge routes patches >30000 chars or >10 files to reviewLarge (head:25-31), so --focus now works on small PRs and is silently ignored on large ones with no error or warning.

findings.title: Restore focus/deep inputs to large-review map and deep prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: This PR deletes `.replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)")` from the deepPrompt chain and removes `focus: bundle.focus, deep: bundle.deep` from mapBundle (lines 87-88). In the base revision those fields were the only route by which the user's focus/deep inputs reached the large-review passes; the explicit `{{FOCUS}}` replacement with a `(none)` default shows prompts/deep.md exposes that token. After the change nothing in review.ts references bundle.focus/bundle.deep, so for every large PR the deep prompt is sent with the literal `{{FOCUS}}` token unresolved (or no focus guidance) and the map pass loses the same context. reviewSmall (src/core/review.ts:51-56) still serializes the entire bundle, so the identical `--focus`/deep option is honored for small PRs and silently ignored for large ones — a size-dependent behavior regression and malformed prompt.

findings.title: Restore {{FOCUS}} substitution in deep prompt
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `.replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)")` leaves the deep template's placeholder unsubstituted. prompts/deep.md contains the literal line `Focus: {{FOCUS}} (if not "(none)", prioritize findings in that area)` (deep.md:96). Every large-review deep pass now sends the raw token `{{FOCUS}}` to the model instead of the user's `--focus` text or the documented fallback `(none)`, so the focus directive is silently ignored on the large path even though the small path still honors it (reviewSmall stringifies the full bundle including focus).

findings.title: Keep focus in mapBundle so map pass can rank focused surfaces
findings.whyItBreaks: Dropping `focus: bundle.focus` from the object passed as `{{BUNDLE}}` to the map pass means the map model never sees the focus field. prompts/map.md:37 explicitly instructs: `If a \`focus\` field is set (not null), rank matching surfaces higher, but do not omit other changed files.` With focus absent from the JSON, that rule can never trigger, so a large PR with `--focus` is no longer steered toward the requested area during hotspot selection. (`deep` is also dropped but map.md has no consumer for it, so that removal alone is benign.)

findings.title: formatDuration can render '1m 60s' after independent rounding
findings.whyItBreaks: minutes is floor(ms/60000) while seconds is round((ms % 60000)/1000); when the remainder rounds up to 60, seconds is never carried into minutes. Verified by evaluating the new expression: 119500 -> '1m 60s', 119999 -> '1m 60s', 59999 -> '60s'. The base expression was self-consistent (round total seconds, then split), so this is a regression introduced by this change. Both call sites render this string into user-facing markdown (src/shared/render.ts:75 per-call and :80 total).

findings.title: formatDuration can render "1m 60s" / "60s" at minute boundary
findings.whyItBreaks: minutes is floored from raw ms (line 90) while seconds is independently rounded from ms % 60000 (line 91), so seconds can round up to 60 while minutes has not carried. ms=119999 -> minutes=1, seconds=Math.round(59999/1000)=60 -> "1m 60s" (base produced "2m 0s"). ms=59500 -> minutes=0, seconds=60 -> "60s" (base produced "1m 0s"). These strings are embedded directly in the rendered review stats at lines 75 and 80, so the malformed duration is user-visible.

findings.title: formatDuration can render "1m 60s" due to independent rounding
findings.whyItBreaks: Minutes are floored from ms and the remainder is rounded separately, so the seconds component can round up to 60 without carrying into minutes. For ms=119999: minutes=Math.floor(119999/60000)=1, seconds=Math.round((119999%60000)/1000)=Math.round(59.999)=60, producing "1m 60s". This fires for any ms whose remainder is >= 59500 (e.g. 119500..119999, and 59500..59999 yields "60s"). The base implementation carried the rounded total seconds through the minute split (totalSeconds=Math.round(ms/1000); minutes=Math.floor(totalSeconds/60)), so it correctly returned "2m 0s" for ms=119999. Result is a user-visible regression in rendered review output.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger silently accepts 0 and empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so zero is no longer rejected. `Number('')`, `Number(' ')`, `Number('0')`, and `Number('0.0')` all coerce to 0; `Number.isInteger(0)` is true and `0 < 0` is false, so the guard falls through and returns 0. The function is exported and its own error string says it `requires a positive integer`, so every eventual caller is forced to treat an invalid/empty argument as a legitimate zero value (e.g. a 0 timeout or 0 count) with no error signal. Previously these inputs threw.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0 despite promising a positive integer
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard was changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` no longer throws and returns 0 (also `Number("") === 0`, so a blank value silently becomes 0). The exported function name, its return contract and the unchanged error message `${label} requires a positive integer` all promise a strictly positive value, so callers receive a non-positive result they cannot distinguish from a valid one — exactly the sentinel/substitution class the review must not rationalize away. The implementation now computes `>= 0` while the carrier promises `> 0`.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0 despite promising a positive integer
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard was `!Number.isInteger(parsed) || parsed <= 0`; changing the second clause to `parsed < 0` makes `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` return 0 instead of throwing. The carrier (function name `parsePositiveInteger` and the unchanged error text `${label} requires a positive integer`) promises positivity, but the body now accepts the non-positive value 0. This is worse than a single bad literal: `Number("")` and `Number(" ")` are both 0, so an empty or whitespace config/CLI value that previously errored now silently parses to 0. Any caller that treats the return as a count/limit/timeout/retry budget can receive 0 where the contract guaranteed >= 1, enabling divide-by-zero, a no-op, an unbounded/zero retry budget, or an immediate-timeout path.
